item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
RRJOLL - From Rrjoll to Himarë, this investigation exposes how Albania's tourism model is driving the transformation of protected areas into luxury “resorts”, enabled by legal reforms and government decisions that favour private interests over environmental protection.

As Albania experiences one of Europe's fastest tourism booms, the country's coastline has become the focus of an unprecedented wave of luxury developments. Behind the promise of economic development, the issue is creating a growing conflict over environmental protection, public resources and decision-making.

This cross-border investigation examines how tourism megaprojects are destroying protected areas, coastal villages and freshwater resources. It explores the environmental consequences of large-scale developments, the legal and political mechanisms enabling them, and their impact on local communities whose livelihoods depend on these fragile ecosystems.

By following multiple case studies - including protected wetlands, coastal construction projects and communities affected by water shortages - it uncovers patterns that extend beyond individual developments, revealing broader structural challenges in Albania's tourism model. It finds that developments promoted as strategic national investments are increasingly expanding into environmentally sensitive areas, while changes in planning and environmental governance have facilitated construction in places previously subject to stronger protection.

The investigation has identified patterns linking public authorities, private investors and regulatory decisions across several major developments that have a real impact on Albania's ecosystem. Together, these findings raise broader questions about transparency, environmental accountability and the long-term sustainability of Albania's tourism model.

Key Findings

  • Albania’s tourism boom is accelerating large-scale construction projects in environmentally sensitive coastal areas.
  • Protected ecosystems are increasingly under pressure from tourism developments promoted as projects of strategic national importance.
  • This model of "development" brings few benefits to local communities, while concentrating profits among a small number of private developers at the expense of Albania's natural resources and ecosystems.
  • Changes in environmental governance and planning procedures have facilitated development in areas previously subject to stronger protection.
  • Changes to legislation governing protected areas have coincided with an acceleration in approvals for large-scale luxury developments, raising serious concerns about transparency and decision-making processes.
  • The investigation identifies a consistent pattern of direct government intervention through legal reforms, strategic investment decisions and planning approvals that has facilitated an unsustainable tourism model, benefiting powerful private interests while accelerating the degradation of Albania's ecosystems.

Methodology

This investigation combined data-driven research with on-the-ground reporting over several months.
The first stage focused on building a comprehensive database of Albania's coastal tourism developments approved between 2015 and 2026. We analysed planning permissions granted by the National Territorial Council (KKT), changes to environmental and planning legislation, strategic investment decisions, environmental impact assessments, and corporate records to identify the investors, developers, architectural firms and public institutions involved in each project.
By cross-referencing these datasets, we identified recurring patterns between legislative changes, the approval of large-scale tourism developments, and environmental concerns repeatedly raised by scientists, NGOs and independent experts. This database also enabled us to select the most representative case studies for further investigation.
The second stage consisted of two weeks of field reporting across Albania. We visited the selected project sites and conducted interviews with local residents, environmental experts, scientists, lawyers, activists, public officials and other stakeholders to assess the environmental and social impacts documented in our data analysis.
Finally, we integrated the documentary research with the field evidence to identify systemic patterns linking legal reforms, strategic investments, planning decisions and environmental degradation. This combined methodology allowed us to move beyond individual case studies and uncover how Albania's current tourism development model is being shaped through the interaction of public policy, private investment and environmental governance.

All the data collected and analysed throughout the investigation can be found on : whoownsthealbaniancoast.com

Themes

  • Corruption
  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Litoral en venta : la maquinaria que privatiza la costa Albanesa, RevistaLate, 27/07/2026
  • “Dosjet e KKT-së” zbulojnë kush e zotëron bregdetin shqiptar, Citizens, 27/07/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Albania

Team members

Marta Moreno Guerrero

Marta Moreno Guerrero is a Spanish freelance journalist.

Lorin Kadiu

Lorin Kadiu is an Albanian media professional with over a decade of experience in journalism and media leadership.

Alexia Galanakis

Alexia is a Chilean freelance journalist based in Spain.

Pablo Fernández Fernández

Pablo Fernández is a Spanish journalist and documentary filmmaker.

Related projects

  • © Jeanna Franke

    Bosnia’s Wood Barons

    SARAJEVO - Around half of Bosnia-Herzegovina is covered by forests and wood is one of the Balkan country’s most valuable natural resources. But instead of developing the nation, some politicians and private companies enrich themselves with the profits of the ‘green gold’. Forests are cut down for private interests and governments and companies in Western-Europe close their eyes to gain cheap wood. 

    Meer lezen
  • © Council for Development and Reconstruction (CDR)

    Tripoli Wastewater Plant: €120m and Two Decades

    TRIPOLI - The investigation looks into the issues that are preventing the expensive wastewater treatment facility in Lebanon from functioning properly.

    Meer lezen
  • © Costanza Musto

    10 Million Tourists A Year In A Small Country

    TIRANA - Albania is experiencing an unprecedented surge in tourism, with more than 7.5 million tourists last year and more than 10 million expected next year. This rapid growth is putting considerable pressure on the country's natural environment.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
GALICIA / IZMIR - As wildfires intensify across the Mediterranean, communities in Spain and Turkey are developing their own strategies to prevent fires, restore damaged ecosystems and protect rural livelihoods, often filling gaps left by public policies.

Across the Mediterranean, wildfires are becoming more frequent, intense and destructive. While public attention often focuses on emergency response and the immediate impacts of fire, less is known about how communities are working to prevent wildfires and restore affected landscapes in the long term.
This cross-border investigation examines grassroots responses to wildfires in Galicia, Spain, and the İzmir region of Turkey. Through field reporting, interviews and visual documentation, the project explores how local communities, farmers, environmental organisations and land managers are developing innovative and traditional approaches to reduce fire risk, regenerate ecosystems and strengthen resilience to climate change.
The investigation also compares two contrasting governance models. In Galicia, communal land ownership structures known as Comunidades de Montes enable collective forest management and prevention initiatives. In Turkey, where forests are largely under state control, community participation is more limited, creating different challenges and opportunities for local action. By highlighting these experiences, the project aims to contribute to broader discussions on wildfire prevention, ecological restoration and climate adaptation across the Mediterranean region.

Key findings

  • Galicia's Comunidades de Montes play a central role in wildfire prevention through collective land management.
  • Nearly half of Galicia's territory is managed under communal ownership structures that encourage local stewardship.
  • Community-led prevention measures include forest clearing, controlled burning and livestock-based fuel management.
  • Turkey's highly centralised forest governance limits the capacity of local communities to participate in prevention efforts.
  • Local initiatives in Turkey exist but often depend on individual leadership and operate within significant legal constraints.
  • Grassroots knowledge and collective action can complement or compensate for shortcomings in institutional wildfire policies.
  • Prevention and ecological restoration receive considerably less attention and investment than fire suppression in both countries.

Methodology

This investigation combines field reporting, data analysis and visual storytelling. The reporting team conducted fieldwork in Galicia (Spain) and the İzmir region (Turkey), spending ten days in each location. During the research, the team interviewed local organisations, environmental NGOs, scientists, community leaders, farmers and residents directly affected by wildfires. We documented prevention, reforestation and land-management initiatives through photography, video and on-the-ground observation. The investigation also draws on forestry databases, land ownership records, academic research, public documents and geospatial analysis tools. All interviews were transcribed, translated where necessary and fact-checked. A comparative approach was used to identify similarities and differences between the two regions, allowing us to examine how governance structures, land ownership models and community engagement influence wildfire prevention and ecological restoration efforts.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Galician communities take on the challenge of revitalizing woodlands to fight wildfires, Bianet, 25/07/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Spain
  • Turkey

Team members

Alba Cambeiro

Alba Cambeiro is a freelance photojournalist based in Galicia, Spain.

Lara Villalón

Lara Villalón is a freelance journalist based in Turkey since 2015.

Mentors

Katarina Zimmer

Katarina (Katya) Zimmer is a an award-winning science and environment journalist based in Berlin.

Related projects

  • © Constance Decorde

    Lucifer's Spell

    LECCE - EVIA - The Mediterranean basin is a hotspot of the climate crisis, with average temperatures rising above global trends. Heat waves, droughts and a combination of anthropogenic factors are provoking new generations of wildfires that are devastating for ecosystems and for human societies.

    Meer lezen
  • © Mary Mwendwa

    Why EU-Banned Pesticides Pose a Risk to Cameroon and Kenya

    NAIROBI / YAOUNDÉ - A cross-border investigation has revealed that pesticides banned in the European Union are still in use in Kenya and Cameroon. These concerning chemicals are readily available to both small- and large-scale farmers, despite them being unaware of their effects.

    Meer lezen
  • © Peter Lipton

    Comparison of Antwerp-Bruges and Rotterdam Ports

    ROTTERDAM / ANTWERP - What is the environmental and health impact of air pollution caused by the (petro)chemical industry in the ports of Antwerp and Rotterdam?

    Meer lezen

item.title: ICMP Honors Vietnam’s Martyrs’ Day and Reaffirms Commitment to Supporting Families of the Missing
item.description:
Hanoi, Vietnam, 28 July 2026 – The International Commission on Missing Persons (ICMP) joined the people and Government of Vietnam in commemorating Martyrs’ Day, honoring those who lost their lives during decades of conflict and recognizing the enduring uncertainty of the families who continue to seek answers about their missing loved ones.

Representing ICMP at the nationally televised commemoration ceremony in Hanoi were ICMP Commissioner Thao Griffiths; Ambassador (ret.) Marc Knapper, former United States Ambassador to Vietnam and newly appointed member of the ICMP Panel of Experts; Chau Nguyen, ICMP Program Manager for Vietnam; and Tom Parsons, ICMP Senior Scientific Advisor. The event, held at the Fallen Soldiers Memorial adjacent to the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum, was attended by General Secretary To Lam, members of the Politburo, and other senior government officials.

On behalf of ICMP, Commissioner Griffiths and Ambassador (ret) Knapper paid tribute to Vietnam’s fallen and to the hundreds of thousands of men and women who remain unaccounted for more than half a century after the end of the war.

“Martyrs’ Day is a powerful reminder that the consequences of conflict do not end when the fighting stops,” said ICMP Commissioner Thao Griffiths. “For many Vietnamese families, the search for truth and answers continues across generations. ICMP is honored to support Vietnam’s efforts to account for the missing and to help ensure that families can finally learn the fate of their loved ones.”

Vietnam faces one of the world’s largest unresolved missing persons challenges. Approximately 200,000 Vietnamese personnel remain unaccounted for, while an estimated 300,000 sets of human remains have yet to be identified. More than 50 years after the war, tropical conditions have significantly degraded skeletal remains, and many close relatives who could provide DNA reference samples are no longer living.

Since 2020, ICMP has partnered with the Center for DNA Identification (CDI), Institute of Biotechnology (IB) of the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology (VAST), and institutions supporting the Vietnam Wartime Accounting Initiative (VWAI) to strengthen Vietnam’s capacity to account for missing persons through the application of advanced DNA technologies and internationally recognized forensic standards.

The partnership has focused on scientific collaboration, laboratory modernization, technology transfer, quality management systems, forensic archaeology and anthropology, secure data management, and training for Vietnamese specialists. The objective is to support the development of a sustainable, nationally owned system capable of operating at scale and independently over the long term.

Working together, CDI-IB-VAST and ICMP, achieved a significant scientific breakthrough  in the application of Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) and advanced nuclear DNA analysis. By examining thousands of Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) markers simultaneously, ICMP and its Vietnamese partners have demonstrated the ability to establish kinship relationships using distant relatives, including third- and fourth-degree family members.

Validation studies undertaken as part of this cooperation have shown that approximately 70 percent of highly degraded skeletal remains can generate DNA profiles suitable for first-degree kinship analysis, while a substantial proportion can support analysis involving more distant relatives. In some cases, DNA profiles containing more than 5,000 SNP markers have enabled comparisons with relatives as distant as great-great-grandchildren.

These advances are now moving from research into operational implementation. Current pilot projects involving approximately 1,000 unidentified graves and more than 2,000 family reference samples are helping demonstrate the feasibility of a future nationwide DNA-led identification program.

“Vietnam’s dedication to account for its missing personnel has been remarkable and inspiring,” Ambassador (ret) Marc Knapper said. “The work Vietnam and its leadership are undertaking today reflects our shared commitment to science, international cooperation, and, most importantly, to the families who have waited decades for answers. ICMP is proud to contribute to this effort with the support of the U.S. Department of State through the Vietnam Wartime Accounting Initiative and in partnership with Vietnamese institutions that are leading this important work.”

As Vietnam commemorates Martyrs’ Day, ICMP reaffirms its support for all efforts aimed at ensuring that those who remain missing are found and that future generations inherit the knowledge that every effort was made to restore the identities of the missing and provide answers to their families. Together with its Vietnamese partners, and with the longstanding support of the U.S. Department of State through the Vietnam Wartime Accounting Initiative, ICMP remains committed to helping Vietnam build a sustainable and nationally owned system to account for the missing.

About ICMP

The International Commission on Missing Persons (ICMP) is a treaty-based intergovernmental organization headquartered in The Hague, the Netherlands. Established in 1996 at the initiative of the G7 Summit, ICMP is mandated to ensure the cooperation of governments and others in locating missing persons resulting from conflict, human rights violations, disasters, organized crime, migration, and other causes. Over nearly three decades, ICMP has supported more than 40 countries in developing internationally recognized systems for accounting for missing persons and has pioneered one of the world’s most advanced large-scale DNA identification capabilities.

About VWAI

The Vietnam Wartime Accounting Initiative is a U.S. government supported effort to help Vietnam find and identify Vietnamese personnel killed or missing from the Vietnam War.

VWAI is comprised of multiple lines of effort, including providing training and equipment so Vietnam can expand its use of DNA analysis in its identification efforts; training and use of archival research to locate prospective graves; support for veteran exchanges; facilitate public-private partnerships to bring in new technologies and resources to expand and support Vietnamese government led efforts.  ICMP is one of the VWAI implementers.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
MISKOLC – Four years after one of Central Europe's most serious river pollution disasters, a cross-border investigation examines what caused the contamination, whether the river has truly recovered, and what lessons remain unanswered.

In 2022, the Sajó River, which flows from Slovakia into Hungary, became the site of one of Central Europe's most serious environmental disasters. Mine water containing arsenic and other heavy metals entered the river system, threatening ecosystems and raising concerns among communities living along its banks. Although emergency measures were introduced, many questions surrounding responsibility, transparency and the long-term environmental consequences have remained unanswered.
This cross-border investigation by Borsod24 and Parameter.sk revisits the disaster several years later to assess what has changed. Through independent laboratory testing, field reporting, interviews with experts, environmental organisations, public officials and local residents, as well as extensive document analysis, the project examines both the causes of the disaster and the current condition of the river.
Beyond reconstructing the events of 2022, the investigation explores whether institutional responses were sufficient, whether pollution risks continue to exist, and what practical measures could prevent similar environmental disasters in the future. By combining scientific evidence with human stories from both sides of the border, the project aims to strengthen public accountability and improve understanding of cross-border environmental protection.

Key Findings

  • The 2022 Sajó River contamination exposed significant weaknesses in environmental monitoring and institutional preparedness.
  • The disaster affected communities in both Slovakia and Hungary, demonstrating the cross-border nature of environmental risks.
  • Independent laboratory measurements are being used to compare current water quality with previous official data.
  • Local residents continue to raise questions regarding transparency, communication and long-term environmental impacts.
  • Experts highlight the importance of improved monitoring systems and stronger international cooperation to prevent similar incidents.

Methodology

The investigation combines documentary research, field reporting, cross-border collaboration and independent scientific verification. The reporting team analysed official documents, historical reporting, environmental data and public records, while conducting interviews with environmental experts, local residents, civil society organisations and public officials. Independent water samples were collected at multiple locations and analysed by an accredited laboratory. item.content:encoded:
MISKOLC – Four years after one of Central Europe's most serious river pollution disasters, a cross-border investigation examines what caused the contamination, whether the river has truly recovered, and what lessons remain unanswered.

In 2022, the Sajó River, which flows from Slovakia into Hungary, became the site of one of Central Europe's most serious environmental disasters. Mine water containing arsenic and other heavy metals entered the river system, threatening ecosystems and raising concerns among communities living along its banks. Although emergency measures were introduced, many questions surrounding responsibility, transparency and the long-term environmental consequences have remained unanswered.
This cross-border investigation by Borsod24 and Parameter.sk revisits the disaster several years later to assess what has changed. Through independent laboratory testing, field reporting, interviews with experts, environmental organisations, public officials and local residents, as well as extensive document analysis, the project examines both the causes of the disaster and the current condition of the river.
Beyond reconstructing the events of 2022, the investigation explores whether institutional responses were sufficient, whether pollution risks continue to exist, and what practical measures could prevent similar environmental disasters in the future. By combining scientific evidence with human stories from both sides of the border, the project aims to strengthen public accountability and improve understanding of cross-border environmental protection.

Key Findings

  • The 2022 Sajó River contamination exposed significant weaknesses in environmental monitoring and institutional preparedness.
  • The disaster affected communities in both Slovakia and Hungary, demonstrating the cross-border nature of environmental risks.
  • Independent laboratory measurements are being used to compare current water quality with previous official data.
  • Local residents continue to raise questions regarding transparency, communication and long-term environmental impacts.
  • Experts highlight the importance of improved monitoring systems and stronger international cooperation to prevent similar incidents.

Methodology

The investigation combines documentary research, field reporting, cross-border collaboration and independent scientific verification. The reporting team analysed official documents, historical reporting, environmental data and public records, while conducting interviews with environmental experts, local residents, civil society organisations and public officials. Independent water samples were collected at multiple locations and analysed by an accredited laboratory. The results are compared with previous official measurements and interpreted with expert assistance. The project also includes on-location video reporting documenting the affected areas and the experiences of local communities.

Themes

  • Environment

item.title: Story From access to opportunity: stories from Southern Bahia, Brazil Earth Regenerative Agriculture Latin America
item.description:
"For years, women had no voice in community decisions and no rights to the land. Today, women are leading change."

When Ailana speaks about her community in Brazil, she is talking about more than leadership.

After ten years of trying, her community secured credit and improved production and livelihoods. Her experience is one of many emerging from Southern Bahia, one of the world's most important cacao-producing regions.

Across the region, smallholder farmers, Indigenous Peoples and other rural communities are gaining access to finance, technical support, new commercial partnerships and opportunities linked to regenerative agriculture and ecosystem restoration. Together, these changes are helping improve livelihoods while protecting biodiversity.

Our partners are helping answer a simple question: what becomes possible when communities gain access to opportunity?
The answers look different across Southern Bahia, but they all begin with securing land rights and the resources and support communities need to thrive.

Opening doors to credit and financial advice

For many rural communities, access to finance is a critical step. Since 2018, our partner Tabôa has worked with smallholder farmers and rural communities across Brazil, helping unlock more than R$25 million (EUR 4.3 million) in credit. Today, the organisation reaches nearly 5,000 people in 44 municipalities.

But access to credit alone is not enough. As one farmer supported by Tabôa explained:

"Receiving credit without technical support is like getting food without knowing how to cook it."

By combining access to finance with technical support, communities can invest in production and livelihoods. In the community of Dois Riachões, farmers who gained access to credit and technical support increased their income by 60%.

Ailana, President of the Nova Vitória Community Association, described the impact in her own community:

"After ten years of trying, we secured credit for our community and were able to improve our production and livelihoods."

Forging partnerships for financial support

Opportunity also comes from stronger connections. Founded with seed funding from Porticus through the Good Energies Foundation in 2018, Conexsus helps Indigenous Peoples, traditional communities and smallholder farmers access finance, markets and technical support.

The organisation is also part of a broader initiative to expand access to subsidised rural credit, helping smallholder farmers adopt regenerative agricultural practices. Its work creates connections that help communities strengthen local enterprises and pursue new opportunities.

Fernando Moretti, Director of Socioeconomic Policies at Conexsus, explains:

"The financial system was designed for large producers, leaving many rural communities behind. We work with banks and government to make credit more accessible, while our social investment fund helps community businesses grow and thrive."

For the Rio de Cima Indigenous tribe, these connections helped unlock new opportunities:

"Before, we were not organised. After some workshops, the cooperative people started to have new ideas, we built new commercial partnerships, and our community thrived."

Accelerating landscape restoration

In Southern Bahia, Belterra works with farmers and communities to transform degraded land into productive, regenerative forests. With support from Porticus’ Good Energies Foundation, the organisation has restored more than 4,500 hectares of land, helped over 200 families access R$10 million in government credit, and supported more than 100 smallholder farms to participate in biodiversity and carbon credit initiatives.

As founder and CEO, Valmir Ortega puts it:

"Keeping the forest standing is also excellent business."

With opportunity comes possibility

While the stories emerging from Southern Bahia are varied, they are connected by a common thread.

For some communities, opportunity depends on access to credit and technical support. For others, it comes through stronger connections to finance and partnerships. 

Together, these stories show what becomes possible when communities can access the resources, relationships and support they need to improve livelihoods while protecting the biodiversity that makes Southern Bahia unique.

item.title: Application
item.description:
Launched by the Palestine Film Institute in May 2025, the Palestine Film Fund provides essential financial and professional support for Palestinian filmmakers worldwide, regardless of where they live or what passport they carry. It was established to ensure that Palestinians have the right to tell their own stories, shape their own narratives and control their own images of experiences, struggles, and hopes.

Applications for the spring cycle are closed.

Our Vision

We are working toward a future where Palestinian cinema is recognised, celebrated and supported on its own terms. Where Palestinian filmmakers have the resources they need to tell the stories today that will become an authentic future archive of Palestinian experiences, told by the community. 

Our Mission

The Fund supports filmmakers, at every stage of their journey, through grants ranging from €3,000 to €15,000 to turn their ideas into films that reach global audiences and establish the solid foundation for a sustainable creative ecosystem where Palestinian voices can thrive. 

Who We Support

Palestinian filmmakers face unique challenges, from restricted access to resources to discrimination against Palestinian narratives. We prioritise supporting those working in the most challenging circumstances: filmmakers based in Palestine,  in lower-income countries, and in regions facing barriers to traditional funding.

How We Support 

The Fund has two submission rounds per year. Starting in 2025, there will be one autumn round opening in the first half of September and one spring round opening in April.

The Fund accepts submissions through a streamlined application process in both English and Arabic to keep it accessible and to allow filmmakers to spend more of their time making films, and less time navigating administrative restrictions.

Grantees will be selected by a revolving international selection committee. Applicants can expect to receive a response within ten to twelve weeks following the submission deadline.

  • Short Films (all stages)

    • Eligible length: up to 30 minutes

    • Eligible stages: all stages (development, production, post-production)

    • Eligible forms: fiction, documentary, animation, hybrid, experimental, essay

    Feature-Length Films

    • Eligible length: longer than 30 minutes

    • Eligible stages: Development, Post-production

    • Not eligible: Production stage

    • Eligible forms: fiction, documentary, animation, hybrid, experimental, essay

    Projects should be original, artistically serious and be intended for television, cinematic, and/or public presentation.

  • Short Films (up to 30 minutes)

    • Development: up to €3,000 (research, concept design, writing, visual references, early creative planning, script development)

    • Production or Post-production: up to €7,000

    Medium- and Feature-length Films (over 30 minutes)

    • Development: up to €5,000 (research, concept design, writing, visual references, early creative planning, script development)

    • Post-production: up to €15,000 (editing, sound design, color grading, festival submission packaging)

    • Production costs are not eligible

    Grant amounts are allocated at the discretion of the selection committee, based on submitted budgets, timeline and feasibility.

  • We will be offering two information sessions for interested filmmakers, scheduled in two different time zones, in April and May. Dates and times will be announced on PFI’s social media channels.

    In case you have any questions please contact the PFF team at fund@palestinefilminstitute.org

    • Applications are open to projects by Palestinian directors residing in Palestine or the diaspora - there are no residence requirements beyond nationality/origin.

    • Applicants do not need citizenship, but must have a recognised link to Palestine.

    • Non‑Palestinians are only eligible if the film director is Palestinian; for example, a non‑Palestinian producer can apply provided the director is Palestinian.

    • Applicants must be 18 years of age or older at the time of application.

    • To apply for feature- or medium-length films, applicants must have previously directed at least one short film.

    • Applicants for short films are welcome regardless of prior directing experience.

    • Co-director teams of which only one person is Palestinian may apply, but the team must prove in their application that the creative relationship is genuine. When applying for a feature, the Palestinian director must have at least directed a short or feature film before.

    • For development, directors and/or producers may apply.

    • For post-production, only the producer may apply. In cases where the producer and director are the same person, this is acceptable.

    • Both individuals and collectives (of directors and producers) may apply, with one designated lead applicant (director or producer) responsible for communication and accountability.

  • No thematic limitations are imposed, but all projects must demonstrate:

    • Ethical and equitable engagement with subjects and collaborators

    • A clear and creative vision outlined in the application form. 

    • Compatibility with PFI’s Community Agreement and
      the Industry Protocol in Times of Genocide

  • The Palestine Film Fund prioritizes applicants:

    • Living and working in Palestine

    • Based in low- and middle-income countries

    • Working in contexts with limited access to traditional film financing
      addressing underrepresented or marginalized perspectives (such as Palestinian refugee camps).

  • All grantees must agree to and uphold the Palestine Film Fund ’s Community Agreement, which includes:

    • Zero tolerance for discrimination, harassment, or exploitation

    • Ethical and equitable storytelling and labor practices

    • Transparent, respectful collaboration

    By applying to the PFF, you agree to uphold the Code of Conduct, you can read it in full here.

    • A logline (max. 80 words)

    • A synopsis (max. 500 words)

    • A project description (max 1500 words)

    • A treatment. For shorts: max 3 pages. For features: max 10 pages. (We understand a treatment as a visual and narrative presentation of your project. This can include images/moods and a narrative structure of your project to help underline your artistic style and approach.)

    • A motivation statement from the director (max. 500 words) if applicable also for the producer

    • A Biography and Filmography of Director and/or Producer

    • An explanation of the project’s current stage and develop/production schedule 

    • A list of partners involved in the project

    • Link to preview material (features: mandatory, shorts: optional)

    • For fiction projects:

      • In development: a script draft (features: mandatory, shorts: optional)

      • In production (only for shorts): a final script is required

    • An overall  budget and financing plan (download template here)

    Unsure what you need to submit? Download our guidelines here:

    • Guidelines & Checklist for Feature Films

    • Guidelines & Checklist for Short Films

    Applications are accepted in both English and Arabic. Visual material is ideally submitted with English subtitles, but this is not mandatory. 

    Please submit via the online form, which is only accessible on this page while submissions are open. Applications sent by email will not be considered. Incomplete applications will not be accepted. 

    • All awarded funds received from the PFI Fund must be expended within 12 months of the date of contract signing in accordance with the contractually agreed upon timeline and deliverables, unless otherwise agreed upon through written extensions. The PFF process does not dictate an overall timeline for the completion of the film.

    • The grant can not cover expenses that occurred before the contractual grant period begins. 

    • For development funding, payment is intended to be made directly to the director. If this is not possible for any reason, a signed statement from the director explaining the reason must be provided. 

    • For post-production funding paid to a non-Palestinian producer, a letter of agreement confirming this arrangement must be provided and signed by the director.

    • Reporting shall be carried out using a simple budget template and narrative report template provided by PFF, and shall include the contractually agreed-upon deliverables (e.g., a trailer, a developed treatment, a final cut, or a completed film).

    • All funds shall be disbursed in two instalments: eighty-five percent (85%) upon execution of the contract, and the remaining fifteen percent (15%) upon submission and acceptance of all required reporting documents and deliverables.

  • Applicants may reapply with the same project up to two additional times if previously rejected.
    Past grantees may reapply with a new project after two full funding cycles (typically one year) have passed.

  • Applicants must be Palestinian directors residing in Palestine or the diaspora - there are no residence requirements beyond nationality/origin.

  • Co-director teams of which only one person is Palestinian may apply, but if applying for a feature project the Palestinian director must have directed and released at least one film, and the team must prove in their application that the creative relationship is genuine.

  • Yes, you can apply if this is your first time directing a short film.

  • No. People applying for feature funding, need to have directed and successfully released at least one short film before.

  • Yes, you can apply for a short film at any stage, and for a feature in development as a director/author. For feature post-production, your producer should apply (unless you are both director and producer). If your set-up is different, please feel free to reach out to us.

  • To be eligible for the fund, the project needs a Palestinian director, but can have a non-Palestinian producer.

  • The fund supports short, medium, and feature-length films across all genres. Short films may apply for development, production, or post-production support, while feature films may apply for development and production support.

  • No. Unfortunately, the PFF does not support series projects.

  • Yes, once you have concluded a funding period successfully, you may apply the same project for another stage of production in another cycle. But please remember, in accordance with the Reapplication Policy of the PFF, past grantees may reapply after two funding cycles only.

  • Projects can be submitted in English and Arabic.

  • Yes, films from any length up to 30 minutes can be submitted as a short film project.

  • No, unfortunately you can not apply with multiple projects in one cycle as a director.

  • Yes, you can apply for more than one as a producer, also if you applied as a director before. 

  • No, unfortunately you can’t apply.

  • Short film projects can apply for up to 3.000 Euro for development, up to 7.000 Euro for production and post-production. For mid-length and feature film projects in development (e.g. research, concept design, writing, visual references, early-stage creative planning) you can apply for up to 5.000 Euro and for post-production (e.g. editing, sound design, color grading, festival submission packaging) you can apply up to 15.000 Euro.

  • Yes, applicants may reapply with the same project up to two additional times if previously rejected. A significant development of the project must be demonstrated and approved by the PFF team before the application can be accepted.

  • After your project is selected you will sign a grantee contract. All amounts will be paid in two instalments, 85% upon signature of contract and the other 15% upon the deliveries (final treatment, final budget, rough cut/ final cut), and a basic overview of incurred and planned expenses.

  • Yes, you must spend the funding received within 12 months of signing the contract; unless an extension was granted in writing.

  • No, unfortunately you can only allocate expenses that are spent after the contractual grant period.

Sawsan Asfari

The Palestine Film Fund exists through meaningful collaboration with film funds, cultural organisations, festivals and foundations who share our vision. We are actively accepting additional institutional partners who can commit to supporting and expanding the global reach of Palestinian storytelling for the long term.

    Please submit via the online form, which is only accessible on this page while submissions are open. Applications sent by email will not be considered. Incomplete applications will not be accepted. 

    • All awarded funds received from the PFI Fund must be expended within 12 months of the date of contract signing in accordance with the contractually agreed upon timeline and deliverables, unless otherwise agreed upon through written extensions. The PFF process does not dictate an overall timeline for the completion of the film.

    • The grant can not cover expenses that occurred before the contractual grant period begins. 

    • For development funding, payment is intended to be made directly to the director. If this is not possible for any reason, a signed statement from the director explaining the reason must be provided. 

    • For post-production funding paid to a non-Palestinian producer, a letter of agreement confirming this arrangement must be provided and signed by the director.

    • Reporting shall be carried out using a simple budget template and narrative report template provided by PFF, and shall include the contractually agreed-upon deliverables (e.g., a trailer, a developed treatment, a final cut, or a completed film).

    • All funds shall be disbursed in two instalments: eighty-five percent (85%) upon execution of the contract, and the remaining fifteen percent (15%) upon submission and acceptance of all required reporting documents and deliverables.

  • Applicants may reapply with the same project up to two additional times if previously rejected.
    Past grantees may reapply with a new project after two full funding cycles (typically one year) have passed.

  • Applicants must be Palestinian directors residing in Palestine or the diaspora - there are no residence requirements beyond nationality/origin.

  • Co-director teams of which only one person is Palestinian may apply, but if applying for a feature project the Palestinian director must have directed and released at least one film, and the team must prove in their application that the creative relationship is genuine.

  • Yes, you can apply if this is your first time directing a short film.

  • No. People applying for feature funding, need to have directed and successfully released at least one short film before.

  • Yes, you can apply for a short film at any stage, and for a feature in development as a director/author. For feature post-production, your producer should apply (unless you are both director and producer). If your set-up is different, please feel free to reach out to us.

  • To be eligible for the fund, the project needs a Palestinian director, but can have a non-Palestinian producer.

  • The fund supports short, medium, and feature-length films across all genres. Short films may apply for development, production, or post-production support, while feature films may apply for development and production support.

  • No. Unfortunately, the PFF does not support series projects.

  • Yes, once you have concluded a funding period successfully, you may apply the same project for another stage of production in another cycle. But please remember, in accordance with the Reapplication Policy of the PFF, past grantees may reapply after two funding cycles only.

  • Projects can be submitted in English and Arabic.

  • Yes, films from any length up to 30 minutes can be submitted as a short film project.

  • No, unfortunately you can not apply with multiple projects in one cycle as a director.

  • Yes, you can apply for more than one as a producer, also if you applied as a director before. 

  • No, unfortunately you can’t apply.

  • Short film projects can apply for up to 3.000 Euro for development, up to 7.000 Euro for production and post-production. For mid-length and feature film projects in development (e.g. research, concept design, writing, visual references, early-stage creative planning) you can apply for up to 5.000 Euro and for post-production (e.g. editing, sound design, color grading, festival submission packaging) you can apply up to 15.000 Euro.

  • Yes, applicants may reapply with the same project up to two additional times if previously rejected. A significant development of the project must be demonstrated and approved by the PFF team before the application can be accepted.

  • After your project is selected you will sign a grantee contract. All amounts will be paid in two instalments, 85% upon signature of contract and the other 15% upon the deliveries (final treatment, final budget, rough cut/ final cut), and a basic overview of incurred and planned expenses.

  • Yes, you must spend the funding received within 12 months of signing the contract; unless an extension was granted in writing.

  • No, unfortunately you can only allocate expenses that are spent after the contractual grant period.

Sawsan Asfari

The Palestine Film Fund exists through meaningful collaboration with film funds, cultural organisations, festivals and foundations who share our vision. We are actively accepting additional institutional partners who can commit to supporting and expanding the global reach of Palestinian storytelling for the long term.

item.title: (Egg)celerator Lab
item.description:
Founded in 2016, this program supports nonfiction filmmakers or filmmaking teams working on their first or second feature-length documentary.

In this year-long program, 9 filmmakers will receive:

  • $40,000 USD in grant funding for the production of their feature-length film

  • Mentorship with Chicken & Egg Films team members

  • Two creative retreats focused on career building and creative development

  • Travel stipend for director and producer upon acceptance to a forum or market during program year

  • Tailored industry meetings and funder connections

  • Peer support from their cohort

(Egg)celerator Lab is made possible in part with support from the New York Community Trust, the Rockefeller Brothers Fund, and through general operating support from our wonderful community of donors and grantmakers.

Filmmakers must meet the following criteria:

  • Must identify as a woman (cis or trans) or gender-expansive director.

    • Our working definition of gender-expansive is that it is an umbrella term that includes any person whose gender identity or gender expression does not comply with the socially defined gender norms and roles of their culture. This includes, but is not limited to, non-binary, trans, third gender/two-spirit, and agender individuals). Please refer to our gender expansion page for more information.

  • Be directing their first or second feature-length (48 minutes or longer) documentary film (hybrid docs are eligible). See the FAQ for Chicken & Egg’s definitions of first-time and second-time directors.

  • Be based anywhere in the world (except for countries/regions which are under comprehensive US sanctions. Further information about US sanctions can be found here).

PROJECT ELIGIBILITY

Projects must meet the following criteria: 

  • Must be a documentary or nonfiction film - hybrid documentaries are eligible. VR, interactive, branded content, or fiction films are not eligible.

    • Our evolving definition of a hybrid documentary is a film that incorporates fictional or scripted elements as a formal device in which it is clear to the viewer which elements are fiction and which are not. The incorporation of fictionalized elements is used as a way to further explore the main themes of the film or even question the nature of ‘fact’ and ‘reality’. Externally the finished film should be intended to be programmed and characterized in the press as documentary or hybrid documentary film, and not as a narrative/fiction film. We do not consider narrative memoir, speculative fiction, or docudramas (dramas that are based on a true story) as hybrid documentaries.

  • Must be intended as a feature-length (48 minutes or longer) film. Short / medium-length films or series are not eligible.

  • Must be in early to mid-production at the time of applying. We recommend that you have between 10-60% of your anticipated footage shot by the date of application.

  • Must be independently produced. Works-for-hire are not eligible, and student films produced in an undergraduate or graduate program are also not eligible.

You do not need a fiscal sponsor to apply for the (Egg)celerator Lab. However, if you are selected for the Lab, you must secure a US fiscal sponsor, or be a 501(c)(3), to receive the funds. If granted, we can help advise on finding a fiscal sponsor. We require prompt response upon communication of results. If granted, there is a 12-week period following notification in which you must secure a fiscal sponsor, and the grant must be disbursed within 2027.

For more information on eligibility, please download this Program & Application Guide and review the FAQs.

Priority will be given to films committed to creating social change and/or uplifting underrepresented stories that challenge mainstream narratives. We support a broad range of issues from the personal to the political that explore a variety of artistic approaches, such as personal, experimental, animated, essayistic, archival, and beyond.

  • Subject Matter and Positionality: The project explores compelling and clear subject matters, themes, and questions, with an awareness of their relevance to our current moment. The story and/or approach aligns with Chicken & Egg Films’ mission and challenges mainstream narratives, conversations, or perceptions. The director demonstrates critical thinking and reflects on their own perspective and biases regarding the subject matter and approach. 

  • Story and Concept: The film features a clear and compelling narrative trajectory or concept, including character arcs where applicable. The director acknowledges the elements that remain unknown and outlines how they will address these gaps. They express a vision for weaving together various elements and arcs into a cohesive and engaging feature. 

  • Artistic Approach: The project shows a distinct and compelling creative vision which conveys a confident directorial voice. The work sample reflects the intended story, style, subject matter, and other project elements. The sample evokes an emotional response and conveys a tone that enhances the storytelling, demonstrating strong use of visuals, sound, music, pacing, and editing. 

  • Feasibility: The application outlines realistic and appropriate activities and a timeline that aligns with the film’s concept and artistic vision. It includes a carefully considered fundraising plan, and the budget is appropriate, reflecting the needs of the proposed activities and timeline.

  • Access and Accountability: The director articulates their access and connection to the story, its participants, and the community involved. They welcome and integrate community feedback and thoughtfully implement processes for accountability that consider physical, mental, cultural safety and beyond. Furthermore, the director reflects on the potential impacts and consequences of the filmmaking process on participants, audiences, crew, and other stakeholders during and after filming. 

Current Work Sample

The current work sample should meet the following criteria:

  • Length: Should be 7-20 minutes of material from the project with which you are applying. We encourage you to not spend extra resources creating a brand new sample for this application if you already have one you have used to apply to other grants/programs. If your current sample is longer than the maximum length of 20 minutes, you can provide timecodes for the portion of the sample you would like reviewers to watch and that best reflects your intended style and approach.

  • Content: Can consist of a combination of the following:

    • 2–3 scene selects/excerpts

    • character strands

    • trailer/teaser/sizzle reel 

    • Note: A trailer alone is neither eligible nor competitive: the sample must contains scenes/character strand, as the work sample is used to evaluate your ability to construct the story.

    • Scenes/excerpts do not need to be in chronological order, so put your strongest material first and separate scenes with title cards. Reviewers are required to watch up to the first 10 minutes in the first round. Work samples will be viewed in full in subsequent rounds.

Prior Work Sample

The purpose of a prior work sample is to give us a sense of the director’s visual style, storytelling ability, ambition, and follow-through. We encourage you to prioritize submitting documentary/nonfiction as prior work.

First-time feature directors:

  • Prior work sample is optional

  • Prior work sample can be of any length or genre, but should be something that you have directed or co-directed

  • Do not include commercial work or PSAs as prior work 

Second-time feature directors:

  • Must submit the first feature-length documentary film that you directed or co-directed as your prior work

  • You can optionally submit 2 additional prior works (of any length or genre) that you have directed or co-directed (this includes student films)

Co-directing teams (first-time/second-time director + more experienced director):

  • The prior work sample submitted should be work from the woman or gender-expansive director who is directing their first or second feature documentary.

Applications to the 2027 (Egg)celerator Lab are currently closed. The deadline to apply was April 29, 2026.

The application for the next cycle of funding will tentatively open in early 2027.  Subscribe to our newsletter to be notified when the next open call is announced.

You can reference the application questions from the past open call via the Program & Application Guide. A recording of the 2027 (Egg)celerator Lab Informational Webinar and Q&A session is available for reference here.

March 4, 2026

2027 (Egg)celerator Lab application opens

April 1, 2026 at 11:59pm ET

Early-bird application deadline - $20 application fee

April 29, 2026 at 11:59pm ET

Regular application deadline - $35 application fee

May - October 2026

Chicken & Egg Films reviews applications in a three-round process

November 2026

All applicants are notified of final decisions.

January-March 2027

First grant installment disbursed

Early 2027

First Cohort Call & Orientation

Spring 2027

First Retreat (5-6 days, in-person - all costs covered by Chicken & Egg Films)

Summer 2027

Second Retreat (5-6 days, in-person - all costs covered by Chicken & Egg Films)

Please note, the program timeline may be subject to change, and any changes will be communicated upon acceptance into the program.

The program includes regular one-on-one calls with our team. Each of the projects will also receive individualized industry strategy consultations and mentorship.

Women (cis and trans) and gender-expansive directors who are in production of their first or second feature-length documentary project are eligible to apply. Co-directing teams, where one director is a woman or gender-expansive filmmaker are also eligible. In this case, please note that the primary contact of the application should be the woman or gender expansive director.

Cis (or cisgender) refers to people whose gender identity aligns with the sex they were given at birth. 

Trans (or transgender) is a term used broadly as an umbrella term to describe anyone whose gender identity differs from their assigned sex. It can also be used more narrowly as a gender identity that reflects a binary gender identity that is “opposite” or “across from” the sex they were assigned at birth. 

Our working definition of gender-expansive is that it is an umbrella term that includes any person whose gender identity (including but not limited to non-binary, trans, third gender/two spirit, agender) or gender expression does not comply with the socially defined gender norms and roles of their culture.

If you are unsure about if you are eligible, please refer to the gender expansion page on our website for additional information.

Grants are $40,000 for each selected film. The grants will be disbursed in installments throughout the program.

Yes. For this application, the questions are in alignment with the Nonfiction Core App 3.1 of the proposal checklist. Our hope is that your responses to these questions will result in material that may be used for other applications as well.

You cannot apply with the same project for both the Research & Development Grant and the (Egg)celerator Lab in the same year. We will disqualify your (Egg)celerator Lab application without review if you have also applied for the R&D grant with the same project in the same year. These opportunities fund different stages of a project. 

Please only apply with the one project that you feel is the best fit for Chicken & Egg Films. Read our guidelines and look at past films we have supported through the (Egg)celerator Lab to get an idea of our interests. You can find links to past cohorts at the end of this webpage. If you really cannot choose between two projects, you can email us at egglab_opencall@chickeneggfilms.org with a short description of both films and ask for our advice. This advice will not impact your application. 

You cannot apply with a film project that you are currently developing in an undergraduate or graduate program. However, if you started a film during a program, and are now independently working on the project, we can consider your film for the Lab.

If the director is a first- or second-time filmmaker, and the project has still not shot more than 60% of its anticipated footage, past applicants may apply again. We urge you to consider how your project has evolved since your last submission and to clearly state how that progress is evident in both your proposal and current work sample.

Due to the continued growth in the number of applications to the (Egg)celerator Lab, we want to give advance notice that starting with the spring 2027 open call, the same project can be submitted only up to 3 times for consideration for the Lab.

If spring 2027 will be your fourth time applying, your project will not be considered. We strongly encourage you to consider whether the current open call is the right moment in your project’s life cycle to submit. The only exception is if you have received a written invitation from the Chicken & Egg Films Program staff explicitly inviting you to reapply.

As a general guideline, we recommend that if you have between 10%-60% of anticipated footage for your film shot, you are in a sweet spot to apply. If you are still in development/pre-production, then the story and sample you submit will not be competitive within the application pool.

Similarly, if you are in late production, you may be looking to finish and premiere before the program year begins.  If you are aiming to reach the rough cut stage by the end of 2026 or by the first quarter of 2027, your project is likely too advanced. 

Filmmakers who have already received support on their first feature-length documentary through the (Egg)celerator Lab are not eligible to apply to the Lab with their second feature-length documentary project. 

If the project was funded through a 2023, 2024, 2025 R&D grant, you can apply to the (Egg)celerator Lab as long as this is still your second feature-length documentary. This is the only instance in which you may apply to the (Egg)celerator Lab with a project that was previously supported by Chicken & Egg Films.

To be eligible, the project must be directed or co-directed by a woman (cis or trans) or gender-expansive filmmaker. Additional team members, such as producers, who are key to the successful development of a project, may collaborate with the director to submit their application. Please note that the primary contact of the application should be the director(s).

As a small nonprofit organization, application fees greatly offset the cost of running our open calls, including paying our external reviewers. We aim to compensate external reviewers–who include filmmakers and industry peers–fairly for their time and expertise.

There is an early-bird fee of $20 if submitting by April 1, 2026 at 11:59pm EST.

There is a regular deadline fee of $35 if submitting by April 29, 2026 at 11:59pm EST.

We understand that a fee can pose a barrier to applying, especially for applicants experiencing financial hardships or who are based in countries with economic instability or unfavorable currency exchange rates.

A fee waiver can be requested by emailing egglab_opencall@chickeneggfilms.org. Please use the subject line: (Egg)celerator Lab - Application Fee Waiver and include a 1-2 sentence explanation for the request. Please make your request early, as the number of waivers available is limited. 

If you are not experiencing financial hardship, we ask that you not request a waiver. We encourage you to apply early to take advantage of the more affordable application fee option.

A first-time director has never completed a feature-length documentary film and is currently working on their first feature-length documentary/nonfiction film. 

A second-time director has already completed and premiered one feature-length documentary film and is currently working on their second feature-length documentary film. If a director has completed and premiered one feature-length documentary film and currently has one or more  works-in-progress, the project they submit will still be considered their second feature as long as it has not been completed or premiered.

You are still considered a first- or second-time director, even if you have the following experience: you have directed multiple shorts or a web series; you have directed feature-length narrative film(s); you have produced feature-length documentary film(s).

Co-directing teams with one first- or second-time co-director and one more experienced co-director are allowed to apply. Please note that the first-or second-time director must also meet the Applicant Eligibility criteria listed above. The prior work sample must be representative of the less experienced filmmaker’s experience.

As a general guideline, we recommend that if you have between 10%-60% of anticipated footage for your film shot, you are in a sweet spot to apply. If you are still in development/pre-production, then the story and sample you submit will likely not be as competitive within the application pool. Similarly, if you are in late production, you may be looking to finish and premiere before the program year begins.  If you are aiming to reach the rough cut stage by the end of 2025 or by the first quarter of 2026, your project is most likely too advanced. 

Only projects in production are eligible to apply because we want to ensure that we have the greatest opportunity possible to make an impact on the production of the project and on the development of the director’s career during the program year. That said, we understand production timelines are dependent on many factors and may change from what you indicate in your application.

As a 501(c)(3), Chicken & Egg Films is not able to support films or projects relating to influencing, directly or indirectly, a political campaign for public office in the US or internationally, regardless of the timing of the release of the film.

If you are unsure about your film’s eligibility based on the above, you can email us at egglab_opencall@chickeneggfilms.org with a description of your film project.

Yes, we require that all submitted materials be in English. This ensures that our reviewers can fully understand and evaluate the application. If any parts of the application are not in English, it may prevent a reviewer from comprehending it in their evaluation of the overall application.

Projects in the early production stage are eligible. At least 10% of shot material is required. No matter what stage of the project, filmmakers are required to submit at least seven minutes of edited footage to apply. Second-time directors must submit a previous work sample. 

Yes. The standard credit we’ll request from grantees in the (Egg)celerator Lab will be “In Association with Chicken & Egg Films.”

Due to our limited staff capacity, we cannot provide one-on-one feedback to all applicants. We do provide some feedback for those whose projects are shortlisted. Chicken & Egg Films believes wholeheartedly in the importance of feedback and is constantly searching for ways to offer more support to all our applicants.

For any questions not addressed on this page, you can email us at egglab_opencall@chickeneggfilms.org.
