item.title: Story Making participation meaningful Education Faith Philanthropy
item.description:
At Porticus, meaningful participation is a moral obligation and the route we chose to create more impactful programmes.

We define meaningful participation as a collaborative process between funders, grantees and people with lived experience who share decision-making power and mutual accountability to ensure positive change. We recognise that all persons involved have equally valuable contributions to bring to the table. Participation is not only a means to an end, it is also the end in itself. 

This is why we want it to be at the centre of our philanthropic practice. However, we don't assume that we have all the answers. The path towards this goal will not always be smooth; meaningful participation often crosses unchartered territory for us. 

As we navigate what it means to be truly participatory, we build on experiences from others, and we share ours. These are the guiding principles we follow, as we aspire to make participation meaningful in our work. 

Making participation meaningful at Porticus

Intention

As we navigate what it means to be truly participatory in our philanthropic practices, we build on experiences from others, and we share ours. This article is the first episode in a series on meaningful participation, directed to the importance of intention. This is one of the 5 guiding principles we follow as we aspire to make participation meaningful in our work.  

For us, intention means doing everything we can to create the space for greater agency and unheard voices to emerge. It is a motivating force that brings focus, purpose and drive to create a more collaborative process with our partners.  

We talked about intention with Terrell Hall (Director at the Transformative in-Prison Workgroup New York) and Sandra van den Heuvel (Programme Manager at Porticus), who both collaborate on Porticus’s Justice Reinvented programme. 

Our intention to create systemic change 

The Justice Reinvented programme in North America created in 2023 is dedicated to expanding the role of community-driven work in California prisons to improve outcomes for all people, especially people in prison and the communities they come from. In California, Justice Reinvented taps into a moment of opportunity where the government has committed to shifting prisons paradigms. Meanwhile, partners of Justice Reinvented seek to ensure that dignity and access to community life will be central to this new vision for the future. 

Drawing from Terrell Hall's firsthand experience of incarceration, his time behind bars ignited a passion for addressing the overlooked issues of mental health, economic disparities and the lack of opportunities for reentry into American society. Recognizing the systemic challenges faced by organizations addressing these issues, Hall got involved with Justice Reinvented upon his release - a joint effort between different partners and Porticus to create a more inclusive and effective approach. 

Revolutionising justice through inclusivity and co-creation 

Justice Reinvented brought voices to the table that had long been ignored. Hall: “The initiative's emphasis on inclusivity and co-creation allowed individuals and communities most affected by the issues to have a significant say in the decision-making process. This participatory practice fosters trust and ensures that the solutions devised were more comprehensive and sustainable. By intentionally bringing together diverse perspectives and stakeholders, the initiative addresses systemic issues on a much deeper level. But to get there, a paradigm shift on the way we are working together is needed. Otherwise, we will be limited by our preconceptions of the way things are - instead of dreaming how things could be truly different.” 

Navigating challenges by building relationships of trust 

The participatory nature of Justice Reinvented had a profound impact on the initiative's approach. The programme brought together diverse partners; including advocates, organizers, researchers, and service-providers, who individually contribute to reform efforts but are testing how working together could yield breakthrough results.  

While participatory work demands more time and effort, it ultimately leads to more authentic solutions and stronger relationships between partners. Building a relationship of trust through participation is one big step to achieve long-term systemic change.

As we navigate these working relationships, obstacles to participation may arise. Terrell underlines the importance of not overlooking the power dynamics between partner and funder and the traditional preconceptions of how this relationship should be. These challenges, however, need to be conquered by the commitment to being inclusive. In Hall’s words: “Despite challenges, such as navigating power dynamics with funders and ensuring equitable compensation for participants, our initiative remains committed to its participatory ethos. We recognize our vital role in effecting meaningful change.” 

Meaningful Participation: Intention

Empathy

Participation is about people - people with their own stories, circumstances and boundaries. When we forget that - despite all good intentions - we can cause harm. Empathy reminds us to approach meaningful participation with profound humility and shared humanity. It is one of the 5 guiding principles we follow as we aspire to make participation meaningful in our work.   

We talked with Komai Alkhateeb (team Lead at Choose Love in Lebanon) and Cory Schiff (Senior Programme Manager at Porticus), about their collaboration on the Collective for Refugee Leadership in the Middle East and North Africa (CRLM), and the importance of empathy in the work they do.

Shifting power to refugee-led organisations   

Since its establishment in 2020, CRLM aims to bring together donors - such as Porticus - and grassroots organisations operating in the MENA region on an equal level playing field. This Collective acknowledges that the power dynamics that exist between donors and refugee-led organisations (RLOs) ultimately affect funding distribution and decision-making processes. With this in mind, CRLM was set up to shift power to RLOs across the region to advance the rights, well-being and security of refugees and their communities. 

Porticus partner Choose Love provides critical support to refugees and displaced individuals across more than 3 countries in the MENA region. Choose Love team lead Komai Alkhateeb is one of the members of CRLM and a key player behind the Collective. He believes in the potential of participatory funding as the best way of acknowledging peoples’ stories and needs. “Refugee leaders and RLOs should be key actors in defining and driving programmatic, advocacy and funding agendas based on their communities’ needs. Therefore, it is crucial that RLOs have decisive power in the way funds are spent.”  

Opening up the dialogue and listening to each other as equals 

Approaching participation with shared humanity means creating the right environment for all stakeholders to be in equal standing in the decision-making arena. Empathy reminds us of the value in respecting the diverse perspectives and priorities of everyone involved. The CRLM understands the importance of this by pushing for collective grant-making, which fosters open dialogues and eye-level conversations between RLOs and donors. Alkhateeb: ‘’We sit together on a regular basis to openly discuss current priorities, and collectively decide on the most pressing regional issues to dedicate resources towards. It’s impressive to see that our partners are able to see beyond their organisations’ scope and focus, and really aim for helping local communities in ways that work for them. Empathy, therefore, plays a key role in understanding each other. It directs us towards our common goals.” 

Understanding the needs of the region and placing them first  

The high needs felt across the MENA region reflects the importance of a well-balanced funding distribution, despite the challenges. “There is uncertainty among both RLOs and donors in terms of resources allocated to the region,” explains Alkhateeb. “Donors are less enthusiastic about funding because of the politicisation of issues. With CRLM, we prove that our work is more important than ever before. And by increasing our partner network - both on the funding as well as sharing capacities and advocating for partners’ work - we will be able to make even more impact in the region.’’ 

Regardless of these challenges, Alkhateeb believes CRLM managed to break down barriers with its participatory approach: “Our work in the collective has fostered empathy and understanding among stakeholders, thereby breaking down power dynamics and supporting genuine collaboration. Simply put, we are empowering RLOs to play a more active role in decision-making processes, leading to projects that are better aligned with community needs and priorities - ultimately improving the lives of those most in need.”  

Meaningful Participation: Empathy

Endurance

Endurance demonstrates both patience and grit to invest in the process and seek out the voices that matter. It’s also the value that ensures we keep asking ourselves important questions - like ‘Who is being left out? Which voices are we missing?’ - and demanding accountability in our response.

We talked about ‘endurance’ with Juan Esteban Belderrain (Senior Programme Manager at Porticus), who collaborates with the Pan-Amazonian Ecclesial Network (REPAM) to support the Catholic Church's mission in caring for human rights and the sustainable development of the Amazon region.

Creating synergies to support the Amazon and its communities

Ever since he joined the ranks of Porticus some 15 years ago, Juan has worked to support the Amazon and the indigenous communities who live there: “Local communities are the best protectors of this unique ecosystem. Our ambition is to enhance their power to create sustainable change.” For this, Juan works with the Catholic Church and REPAM (a network that brings together local and international organisations, missionaries, and congregations) to support grassroots organisations whose aim is to defend the rights of these communities.

Endurance has been crucial to ensure the success of Porticus’ collaboration with the Church and REPAM. Throughout the years, this working relationship observed important milestones in which some traditional narratives of the Church were overcome and started to include the voices of who those know best what the Amazon needs to flourish.

Overcoming traditional top-down views

In Juan’s experience, the Church plays an elemental in local development across Latin America – also in the Amazon region: “Their influence can be felt in the smallest of villages, and the Church is very invested in realising positive change.”

The Church is an enormous institution with many layers of complexity and divisions of powers. In this working relationship, Porticus focuses on balancing the shared ambition of fostering the mission of the Church and its contribution to local development in the region while still being critical of how the support given to the communities can be more participatory and inclusive.

“While the Church traditionally takes a more top-down approach to realise change, Porticus believes in a more participatory way of working with local communities – especially with underrepresented groups. With REPAM, we managed to find a balance between both approaches. An interesting example is the way that this network is organised. As the Church is traditionally a male-centred institution, the active role of indigenous women in decision-making processes in these networks is a significant step forward.”

A few well-established narratives sometimes need to be challenged also through a bottom-up approach: “For many local communities, the Church has a mythical status. Overcoming these century-long power dynamics is not easy. It is important to respect the complexities of local norms and customs and recognise the power asymmetries between institutions and communities.  Navigating these differences also help us to be critical and flexible about the ways we work with our partners.”

Endurance becomes key to making the most out of this working relationship. Encouraging changes in institutional structures such as the Church, and adapting ways of working to maximise the positive change created takes time and patience: ‘’We have different points of view, which could complicate matters. But we always look for those elements we align on - which are a lot.”

In 2019, Pope Francis called for a Universal Synod in Rome on the Amazon to give international visibility to this region's pastoral, social and environmental challenges. 87,000 people participated in the previous work organised by REPAM. For the first time in the history of the Church, indigenous peoples were present at the Synod, exposing their problems and proposals. It was there that the Pope saw, in his words, a new Church "where the periphery becomes the centre." Now, he wants to extend this proposal to the global Church through the current Synod on "Synodality: communion, participation and mission”. “I’d like to think that it is an outcome of our collective endurance.”

Meaningful Participation: Endurance

Trust

Taking a participatory approach isn’t linear, and it isn’t easy. We know there will be bumps along the way. Our goal is to fail forward; to try, to learn (from our own journey and from others), and to grow. If we trust the process, and express that same deep trust to people and partners, success will follow.   

We spoke with Shripathi Hadigal (Regional Resource Mobilization Manager at Restless Development India) and Vrinda Kapur (Programme Manager for Porticus), about the importance of trust in their collaboration on the Fair Urban Transition (FUT) programme in Bangalore, India.

Pressing issues need collaborative measures 
 
At the heart of Porticus and its FUT programme partners in India lies a shared conviction: communities should lead in the development of the climate policies which will affect them. We spoke to one of the ten programme partners, Restless Development, that enables the involvement of young people in decision-making on crucial issues like Climate Justice. Both parties have partnered for this programme alongside other local organisations to help ensure that the transition to a carbon-free future in cities like Bangalore is fair to all. 

The final phase of the FUT programme, which will reach its end in 2025, has been co-designed by all partners, who collectively decided where and how to allocate resources while keeping the best interests of the Bangalore communities in mind. Vrinda: “We wanted partners to make decisions together, including allocation of funds to themselves. By bringing our partners to the table to co-develop a narrative, activities, timeline and budget, we collaboratively focus on the most pressing issues, and in those areas that need most attention.” 

Welcoming this more collaborative way of working challenged all ten partners involved to trust each other at a deeper level. It was not just placing faith in the individuals driving the project forward, but also about trusting the process itself and its outcomes. In Vrinda’s words: “It takes courage and an open mind for all of us to work together on issues. We needed to trust on each other’s expertise and input to make decisions that might not be particularly relevant for one specific organisation, but that are most impactful for the communities and our common goal: A flourishing Bangalore where climate policies are inclusive, deliberate and participatory.’’ 

Meaningful participation takes time  

Forging stronger collaborations is not always easy. It takes time to create spaces where all partners can contribute meaningfully and understand that conflicts are bound to emerge in such spaces. On this, Vrinda shares: “It took us 4 months to deliberate and co-create the final phase of this programme. While we agreed on our vision for Bangalore, we also had difference in opinions around what our priorities could be for this limited period of time of this programme, ways of collaborating and allocation of the limited funds." These are difficult decisions, and required different methods to reach consensus. “In addition to having bilateral conversations with each organisation, to support this process further, we worked with an external facilitator who created a safe space to foster trust and vulnerability amongst delegates from these organisations. This way, we got to see the individuals beyond the face of the organisation, which helped us in breaking down barriers and truly understanding each other.” 

Shripathi explains the benefit of trusting and listening to different people, experts and organisations. “Every partner brings something else to the table. Some are actively involved with local communities, while others take a more scientific approach to specific issues. This might sound conflicting, but it allows us all to look at the world through different lenses and facilitate the co-creation of more impactful and tailored solutions. For example, we work together with three organisations which take different approaches to minimise water-related issues in Bangalore to map the city wards in a more holistic way. In this project, researchers, decision-makers and the local community all work together to help improve the accessibility of water in different parts of the city and minimise flooding risks.’’

Although the current programme is ending next year, Vrinda and Shripathi along with other nine implementing partners are working together to ensure that this participatory way of collaborating between organisations continues in the future. Trusting the process and trusting each other plays a crucial role in achieving this.

Meaningful Participation: Trust

Modesty

Systemic change cannot happen without being open about where power lies and how to navigate and negotiate its distribution. When we talk about being modest, we are bringing awareness to our relative power in meaningful participation relationships, and committing to using it responsibly - and challenging it at every opportunity we get.  

Dian​a​ Nyamu (Programme Manager at Porticus) and Justin Abumbah (Program Lead at Cohere) talk with us about the importance of modesty in their daily work in Kenya’s Kakuma refugee camp, where they support refugee-led organisations (RLOs) to realise sustainable change. 

Modesty as a catalyst for collaboration 

Backed by Porticus, Cohere supports eight RLOs that​ have ​​community ​​interventions ​​     ​directed ​to ​advocate for better education outcomes for refugee children in Kakuma. By facilitating collaboration and sharing of best practices, Cohere empowers RLOs to become active agents of change, transcending their formerly perceived passive roles in the humanitarian sector.  

Modesty plays a crucial role in this collaboration and encourages the working relationship between Cohere, Porticus and RLOs to be participatory. Openness to acknowledge power dynamics, but respecting and learning from each other as equals motivates all parties to effectively work towards a common cause. Nyamu reiterates: “RLOs are not viewed simply as recipients of grants, but as innovators who have ideas and solutions.”  

Abumbah emphasises the importance of participation in achieving positive impact: “By localising interventions, amplifying contextualised solutions and empowering community leaders to exercise their agency, we ensure that initiatives are not only locally relevant, but ​they are ​also sustained long after our departure. This participatory ethos not only enhances programme effectiveness, but also fosters a sense of ownership among beneficiaries.” 

Listening and respecting partners’ expertise and efforts 

Guided by a strong set of principles - including modesty, Porticus makes sure to not cast its shadow over partners’ efforts. “We anonymously support on-the-ground initiatives, providing flexible funding, while maintaining a low profile,” says Nyamu. “Cohere excels in community engagement, collaborating with Porticus and the RLOs to co-design interventions building on the lived experience of the community members.  As a result, RLOs have the freedom to use the funds in a way that best supports and meets the ​education ​needs of the​ ​learners in Kakuma.” 

Meanwhile, Porticus takes a step back. “We practice open Communication and Listening,” says Nyamu. “We maintain an open dialogue with Cohere to share updates, successes, and failures. Through regular discussions, we aim to dismantle traditional power dynamics where partners report to Porticus in a top-down manner. This approach fosters a system of reciprocity and mutual accountability. Moreover, Porticus frequently visits the refugee camp to engage with RLOs and ground-level partners. Through shared experiences, we collaboratively address challenges enriching the work of these RLOs.” 

A​b​umbah adds: “Modesty is ingrained in the way Porticus listens to us as a partner. Their focus is not solely directed to concrete project numbers, but rather the overall results or project outcomes that we hope to jointly achieve together with the RLOs and community leaders.  Although a distinction between a provider of grants and a grantee is inevitable, I feel that Porticus is an equal partner journeying with us for the long haul towards a common objective. That​ has ​been a new experience for me with a funder.” 

Meaningful Participation: Modesty
item.content:encoded:
At Porticus, meaningful participation is a moral obligation and the route we chose to create more impactful programmes.

We define meaningful participation as a collaborative process between funders, grantees and people with lived experience who share decision-making power and mutual accountability to ensure positive change. We recognise that all persons involved have equally valuable contributions to bring to the table. Participation is not only a means to an end, it is also the end in itself. 

This is why we want it to be at the centre of our philanthropic practice. However, we don't assume that we have all the answers. The path towards this goal will not always be smooth; meaningful participation often crosses unchartered territory for us. 

As we navigate what it means to be truly participatory, we build on experiences from others, and we share ours. These are the guiding principles we follow, as we aspire to make participation meaningful in our work. 

Making participation meaningful at Porticus

Intention

As we navigate what it means to be truly participatory in our philanthropic practices, we build on experiences from others, and we share ours. This article is the first episode in a series on meaningful participation, directed to the importance of intention. This is one of the 5 guiding principles we follow as we aspire to make participation meaningful in our work.  

For us, intention means doing everything we can to create the space for greater agency and unheard voices to emerge. It is a motivating force that brings focus, purpose and drive to create a more collaborative process with our partners.  

We talked about intention with Terrell Hall (Director at the Transformative in-Prison Workgroup New York) and Sandra van den Heuvel (Programme Manager at Porticus), who both collaborate on Porticus’s Justice Reinvented programme. 

Our intention to create systemic change 

The Justice Reinvented programme in North America created in 2023 is dedicated to expanding the role of community-driven work in California prisons to improve outcomes for all people, especially people in prison and the communities they come from. In California, Justice Reinvented taps into a moment of opportunity where the government has committed to shifting prisons paradigms. Meanwhile, partners of Justice Reinvented seek to ensure that dignity and access to community life will be central to this new vision for the future. 

Drawing from Terrell Hall's firsthand experience of incarceration, his time behind bars ignited a passion for addressing the overlooked issues of mental health, economic disparities and the lack of opportunities for reentry into American society. Recognizing the systemic challenges faced by organizations addressing these issues, Hall got involved with Justice Reinvented upon his release - a joint effort between different partners and Porticus to create a more inclusive and effective approach. 

Revolutionising justice through inclusivity and co-creation 

Justice Reinvented brought voices to the table that had long been ignored. Hall: “The initiative's emphasis on inclusivity and co-creation allowed individuals and communities most affected by the issues to have a significant say in the decision-making process. This participatory practice fosters trust and ensures that the solutions devised were more comprehensive and sustainable. By intentionally bringing together diverse perspectives and stakeholders, the initiative addresses systemic issues on a much deeper level. But to get there, a paradigm shift on the way we are working together is needed. Otherwise, we will be limited by our preconceptions of the way things are - instead of dreaming how things could be truly different.” 

Navigating challenges by building relationships of trust 

The participatory nature of Justice Reinvented had a profound impact on the initiative's approach. The programme brought together diverse partners; including advocates, organizers, researchers, and service-providers, who individually contribute to reform efforts but are testing how working together could yield breakthrough results.  

While participatory work demands more time and effort, it ultimately leads to more authentic solutions and stronger relationships between partners. Building a relationship of trust through participation is one big step to achieve long-term systemic change.

As we navigate these working relationships, obstacles to participation may arise. Terrell underlines the importance of not overlooking the power dynamics between partner and funder and the traditional preconceptions of how this relationship should be. These challenges, however, need to be conquered by the commitment to being inclusive. In Hall’s words: “Despite challenges, such as navigating power dynamics with funders and ensuring equitable compensation for participants, our initiative remains committed to its participatory ethos. We recognize our vital role in effecting meaningful change.” 

Meaningful Participation: Intention

Empathy

Participation is about people - people with their own stories, circumstances and boundaries. When we forget that - despite all good intentions - we can cause harm. Empathy reminds us to approach meaningful participation with profound humility and shared humanity. It is one of the 5 guiding principles we follow as we aspire to make participation meaningful in our work.   

We talked with Komai Alkhateeb (team Lead at Choose Love in Lebanon) and Cory Schiff (Senior Programme Manager at Porticus), about their collaboration on the Collective for Refugee Leadership in the Middle East and North Africa (CRLM), and the importance of empathy in the work they do.

Shifting power to refugee-led organisations   

Since its establishment in 2020, CRLM aims to bring together donors - such as Porticus - and grassroots organisations operating in the MENA region on an equal level playing field. This Collective acknowledges that the power dynamics that exist between donors and refugee-led organisations (RLOs) ultimately affect funding distribution and decision-making processes. With this in mind, CRLM was set up to shift power to RLOs across the region to advance the rights, well-being and security of refugees and their communities. 

Porticus partner Choose Love provides critical support to refugees and displaced individuals across more than 3 countries in the MENA region. Choose Love team lead Komai Alkhateeb is one of the members of CRLM and a key player behind the Collective. He believes in the potential of participatory funding as the best way of acknowledging peoples’ stories and needs. “Refugee leaders and RLOs should be key actors in defining and driving programmatic, advocacy and funding agendas based on their communities’ needs. Therefore, it is crucial that RLOs have decisive power in the way funds are spent.”  

Opening up the dialogue and listening to each other as equals 

Approaching participation with shared humanity means creating the right environment for all stakeholders to be in equal standing in the decision-making arena. Empathy reminds us of the value in respecting the diverse perspectives and priorities of everyone involved. The CRLM understands the importance of this by pushing for collective grant-making, which fosters open dialogues and eye-level conversations between RLOs and donors. Alkhateeb: ‘’We sit together on a regular basis to openly discuss current priorities, and collectively decide on the most pressing regional issues to dedicate resources towards. It’s impressive to see that our partners are able to see beyond their organisations’ scope and focus, and really aim for helping local communities in ways that work for them. Empathy, therefore, plays a key role in understanding each other. It directs us towards our common goals.” 

Understanding the needs of the region and placing them first  

The high needs felt across the MENA region reflects the importance of a well-balanced funding distribution, despite the challenges. “There is uncertainty among both RLOs and donors in terms of resources allocated to the region,” explains Alkhateeb. “Donors are less enthusiastic about funding because of the politicisation of issues. With CRLM, we prove that our work is more important than ever before. And by increasing our partner network - both on the funding as well as sharing capacities and advocating for partners’ work - we will be able to make even more impact in the region.’’ 

Regardless of these challenges, Alkhateeb believes CRLM managed to break down barriers with its participatory approach: “Our work in the collective has fostered empathy and understanding among stakeholders, thereby breaking down power dynamics and supporting genuine collaboration. Simply put, we are empowering RLOs to play a more active role in decision-making processes, leading to projects that are better aligned with community needs and priorities - ultimately improving the lives of those most in need.”  

Meaningful Participation: Empathy

Endurance

Endurance demonstrates both patience and grit to invest in the process and seek out the voices that matter. It’s also the value that ensures we keep asking ourselves important questions - like ‘Who is being left out? Which voices are we missing?’ - and demanding accountability in our response.

We talked about ‘endurance’ with Juan Esteban Belderrain (Senior Programme Manager at Porticus), who collaborates with the Pan-Amazonian Ecclesial Network (REPAM) to support the Catholic Church's mission in caring for human rights and the sustainable development of the Amazon region.

Ever since he joined the ranks of Porticus some 15 years ago, Juan has worked to support the Amazon and the indigenous communities who live there: “Local communities are the best protectors of this unique ecosystem. Our ambition is to enhance their power to create sustainable change.” For this, Juan works with the Catholic Church and REPAM (a network that brings together local and international organisations, missionaries, and congregations) to support grassroots organisations whose aim is to defend the rights of these communities.

Endurance has been crucial to ensure the success of Porticus’ collaboration with the Church and REPAM. Throughout the years, this working relationship observed important milestones in which some traditional narratives of the Church were overcome and started to include the voices of who those know best what the Amazon needs to flourish.

Overcoming traditional top-down views

In Juan’s experience, the Church plays an elemental in local development across Latin America – also in the Amazon region: “Their influence can be felt in the smallest of villages, and the Church is very invested in realising positive change.”

The Church is an enormous institution with many layers of complexity and divisions of powers. In this working relationship, Porticus focuses on balancing the shared ambition of fostering the mission of the Church and its contribution to local development in the region while still being critical of how the support given to the communities can be more participatory and inclusive.

“While the Church traditionally takes a more top-down approach to realise change, Porticus believes in a more participatory way of working with local communities – especially with underrepresented groups. With REPAM, we managed to find a balance between both approaches. An interesting example is the way that this network is organised. As the Church is traditionally a male-centred institution, the active role of indigenous women in decision-making processes in these networks is a significant step forward.”

A few well-established narratives sometimes need to be challenged also through a bottom-up approach: “For many local communities, the Church has a mythical status. Overcoming these century-long power dynamics is not easy. It is important to respect the complexities of local norms and customs and recognise the power asymmetries between institutions and communities.  Navigating these differences also help us to be critical and flexible about the ways we work with our partners.”

Endurance becomes key to making the most out of this working relationship. Encouraging changes in institutional structures such as the Church, and adapting ways of working to maximise the positive change created takes time and patience: ‘’We have different points of view, which could complicate matters. But we always look for those elements we align on - which are a lot.”

In 2019, Pope Francis called for a Universal Synod in Rome on the Amazon to give international visibility to this region's pastoral, social and environmental challenges. 87,000 people participated in the previous work organised by REPAM. For the first time in the history of the Church, indigenous peoples were present at the Synod, exposing their problems and proposals. It was there that the Pope saw, in his words, a new Church "where the periphery becomes the centre." Now, he wants to extend this proposal to the global Church through the current Synod on "Synodality: communion, participation and mission”. “I’d like to think that it is an outcome of our collective endurance.”

Meaningful Participation: Endurance

Trust

Taking a participatory approach isn’t linear, and it isn’t easy. We know there will be bumps along the way. Our goal is to fail forward; to try, to learn (from our own journey and from others), and to grow. If we trust the process, and express that same deep trust to people and partners, success will follow.   

We spoke with Shripathi Hadigal (Regional Resource Mobilization Manager at Restless Development India) and Vrinda Kapur (Programme Manager for Porticus), about the importance of trust in their collaboration on the Fair Urban Transition (FUT) programme in Bangalore, India.

Pressing issues need collaborative measures

The final phase of the FUT programme, which will reach its end in 2025, has been co-designed by all partners, who collectively decided where and how to allocate resources while keeping the best interests of the Bangalore communities in mind. This way, we got to see the individuals beyond the face of the organisation, which helped us in breaking down barriers and truly understanding each other.” 

Shripathi explains the benefit of trusting and listening to different people, experts and organisations. “Every partner brings something else to the table. item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
BRESCIA / MARSEILLE / ZWIJNDRECHT - From Italy to Belgium and France, the European principle of environmental liability is only applied by halves: it requires companies to make contaminated private sites safe, but leaves citizens and communities to bear the final cost.

The European Union's Polluter Pays Principle promises a simple idea: those responsible for environmental damage should bear the costs of preventing and remedying it. In practice, however, decades of industrial contamination have left communities across Europe carrying billions of euros in environmental, economic and health costs, while many polluters have avoided full accountability. From Brescia in Italy to Zwijndrecht in Belgium and Marseille in France, communities have been exposed to PCBs, PFAS and heavy metals- persistent pollutants linked to increased cancer rates and long-term health damage. Yet people living near these contaminated sites keep asking the same question: if the Polluter Pays Principle exists, why are local communities still paying the highest price decades later?

Part of the answer lies in the way the principle has been implemented. EU environmental legislation has largely focused on ensuring that polluters finance the prevention and remediation of environmental damage. But for residents living with the consequences of contamination – ill health, falling property values and years of financial uncertainty – obtaining compensation relies on lengthy legal battles, with no guarantee of success. As a result, while polluted land may eventually be cleaned up, the human costs are frequently borne by the communities themselves.

Key Findings:

  • Although, under the Polluter Pays Principle (PPP), polluters may eventually bear the costs of environmental remediation, the European Union still lacks a horizontal legal framework that uniformly regulates compensation for health damage caused by environmental contamination.
  • The PPP primarily focuses on repairing environmental damage, rather than compensating individuals and communities for the broader social and economic consequences of pollution.
  • As a result, important forms of harm often remain unaddressed, including: loss of income and livelihoods for people living near contaminated sites, long-term health costs and medical expenses, reduced property values and economic decline in affected communities and psychological and social impacts associated with prolonged environmental exposure.
  • A representative example is the case of Pierino Antonioli in Brescia, a farmer who lost the ability to cultivate his land and raise livestock because of contamination, while receiving no compensation for his economic losses. Pierino is also being treated for his fifth tumour.
  • In Marseille, although a court ordered the state to require the site's owner, Ginkgo, to carry out remediation, little has happened, as the company has sought to limit the scope and cost of the clean-up. Meanwhile, despite unusually high cancer rates and official recommendations that some residents avoid using their contaminated gardens, residents' claims for compensation have been rejected.
  • In Zwijndrecht, especially in the so-called 'red zone', the area closest to the 3M plant, nobody has received any compensation. Residents' blood is saturated with PFAS – including that of newborn babies. In 2022, €571 million was allocated by the Flemish government and 3M, but not a single penny of this amount is earmarked for damage to residents' health.

Methodology:

This investigation combines documentary research with field reporting. It is based on company registry reports, interviews with affected communities living near contaminated sites, and a review of legal documents related to environmental litigation and court proceedings.

Photo : Pierino Antonioli's empty barn in Brescia, abandoned since 2001 after Caffaro contamination forced him to stop farming and raising livestock. He has never received compensation for his losses. Credits: Stefano Nicoli

  • Environment

  • Chi inquina non paga: cosa succede alle comunità quando le aziende responsabili ignorano le leggi europee, VoxEurop, 17/07/2026
  • 污染者不买单：当企业无视欧洲法律时，社区会遭遇什么, The newcomers, 20/07/2026

PRINT

  • In Europa chi inquina non paga, L'Espresso Magazine, 17/07/2026, p.68

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Belgium
  • France
  • Italy

Team members

Nuri Fatolahzadeh

Nuri Fatolahzadeh is an independent Italian-Iranian reporter based in Lombardy.

Federica Tessari

Federica Tessari is an investigative Italian journalist and reporter.

Luigi Simonelli

Luigi Simonelli is an Italian journalist living in France.

Teresa Di Mauro

Teresa Di Mauro is an Italian independent journalist.

Related projects

  • © Gerard Stolk (via Flickr)

    The Art of Looking Away

    ANTWERP - The pollution around the 3M plant near Antwerp (Belgium) has been known for years. Yet the PFOS scandal did not erupt in Flanders until the spring of 2021.

    Meer lezen
  • © Olga Khvorost

    Ukraine delays industrial pollution reforms. What it means for Europe

    KYIV -  This story examines the relationship between the pace of Ukraine's reforms regarding industrial pollution and the country's prospects for integration into the European Union, particularly in the promising energy sector.

    Meer lezen

  • Dirty Money for Clean Rivers

    BUCHAREST - For almost 9 years, Romania has been criticised and monitored by the European Commission for allowing the large-scale destruction of several mountain rivers for the purpose of building micro-hydropower plants, without complying with the Water Framework and Habitats Directives.

This investigation combines documentary research with field reporting. It is based on company registry reports, interviews with affected communities living near contaminated sites, and a review of legal documents related to environmental litigation and court proceedings.

Photo : Pierino Antonioli's empty barn in Brescia, abandoned since 2001 after Caffaro contamination forced him to stop farming and raising livestock. He has never received compensation for his losses. Credits: Stefano Nicoli

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
ATHENS / RAVENNA / VALENCIA - The European research project UnderSec links surveillance of the Greek port of Lavrio, Ravenna and Valencia to technologies "battle tested" by the Israel Defence Forces, amid a lack of transparency and the circumvention of environmental protection regulations.

The Authority of the small port of Lavrio (near Athens) is a partner in the UnderSec project funded with almost 6 million euros of research European funds (Horizon), and underwater cybersecurity technologies are being tested here. The project involves 22 members, all European except three Israeli entities: the Israeli Ministry of Defence, Rafael Advanced Systems, one of the country’s leading arms manufacturers, and Tel Aviv University. Currently state-controlled, the port of Lavrio has been undergoing privatisation for about a year, with the sale of 51% of the shares of the Port Authority. Among the interested buyers is also Israel Shipyards, an Israeli company deeply involved in Israel’s industrial and military ecosystem.

Among the technologies tested in the UnderSec project there is also the Broadlink modem, owned by Rafael Advanced Systems, an underwater acoustic communication system designed to transmit audio, images and video between submarines, marine drones and sensors. According to technical specifications, these modems can operate in the low–mid frequency range between 4 and 10 kHz and in the mid–high frequency range between 15 and 35 kHz, frequencies that may interfere with those used by many dolphin species. According to the official brochure, it has been “battle tested”, and is already in use on underwater drones, special forces vessels and Israeli military divers. It is not excluded that it has also been used to intercept and attack the flotilla.

Although the port of Lavrio falls within the Natura 2000 SPA site “Strait of Makronisos”, many of the technologies used in the UnderSec project include low-, medium- and high-frequency sonar, acoustic modems, loudspeakers, drones, sensors generating electromagnetic waves, radioactive neutron generators, in short all instruments that - according to experts - have impacts on the marine environment and fauna. The investigation has unveiled that environmental authorization required by the Greek law for such a project has not been requested. The lead researcher on the UnderSec project for Rafael Advanced Systems (Oren Gal, head of the drone swarm laboratory at the University of Haifa) also works at MIT in Boston on two projects funded by the Israeli minister of Defence, which, according to the report “MIT Science for Genocide”, may have contributed to the genocide in Gaza.

Key Findings :

  • The port authorities of Valencia and Lavrio (Athens) between March and June 2026 allowed the testing of the Broadlink underwater communications modem “war-tested” by the Israeli company Rafael Advanced Systems, to integrate it with sensors and autonomous underwater vehicles from companies in Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Greece.
  • In Greece, whose companies and universities received around two-thirds of UnderSec's funding, the test was carried out in cooperation with the Greek armed forces, according to the UnderSec website, but the Greek navy denies any involvement.
  • No environmental evaluation was provided by the project coordinator, despite the environmental risks associated with the experiment, which used "explosive and narcotic simulants" and radioactive materials, and despite the fact that the port of Lavrio is a Natura 2000 protected site.
  • The algorithms that process the data from the various sensors were developed for Rafael by Professor Oren Gal, head of the Drone Swarm Laboratory at the University of Haifa, and former founder and technology director of the Israeli Navy's Autonomy and Data Science Research and Development branch , and later of the Department of Defense, Development, and Reconstruction at the IMoD (Israeli Ministry of Defense). Since 2019, he has also been working on research at MIT in Boston funded by the IMoD, which has military applications in "drone aerial bombardments, protest surveillance, the pursuit of fleeing targets, and the use of tear gas during home demolitions," as highlighted in the MIT for Palestine network's "MIT Science for Genocide" report.
  • Although the European Commission has reiterated that it is "a civil security research project funded under Cluster 3 (Civil Security for Society) of Horizon Europe," UnderSec was born and developed with strong ties to NATO and with the goal of commercialization in military contexts. Nato navies and the Saudi Arabian Navy and Army were interested in monitoring the project and acquiring the final product.
  • In the last months as the “Broadlink” modem was being tested as part of Undersec, DSIT, a Rafael subsidiary specializing in sonar systems and underwater security, presented a new Underwater Domain Awareness (UDA) solution for continuous, long-range underwater monitoring. Broadlink is among its technologies publicized in the specialized press. On April 6, 2026, DSIT Solutions announced the signing of an agreement to supply its Tactical Underwater Domain Awareness sonar systems to a "leading" NATO navy.
  • Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft, coordinator of Undersec, signed an agreement in March 2025 with the IIA (Israel Innovation Authority, an organization dependent on the Israeli government with offices in Brussels) to promote Israeli technologies in Europe through projects such as Horizon Europe. The collaboration, signed in the midst of the genocide in Gaza, suggests that UnderSec can represent a model, which Germany intends to use to include technologies and artificial intelligence “made in Israel” in German and European rearmament.

Themes

  • Environment

  • Israel's defence industry is expanding into the Greek seabed, MIIR, 11/07/2026
  • Η πολεμική βιομηχανία του Ισραήλ στον ελληνικό βυθό του Λαυρίου, Η Εφημερίδα των Συντακτών (EFSYN), 12/07/2026

  • Yunanistan’da İsrail ile deniz altında çevreye zararlı askeri test yapıldığı iddiası, Anadolu Ajansı, 11/07/2026

    HEBRON - In a bid to combat a wave of lone-wolf attacks, Israel has arrested hundreds of Palestinian youths suspected of being potential would-be terrorists over the past 18 months. Many, if not most, of the Palestinians arrested have been singled out by a computerised prediction system developed by the Israeli authorities. According to Israeli officials, some of the individuals were arrested on their way to carry out an attack, but others may not have even fully decided to commit an attack at the time of their arrest.

    Why EU-Banned Pesticides Pose a Risk to Cameroon and Kenya

    NAIROBI / YAOUNDÉ - A cross-border investigation has revealed that pesticides banned in the European Union are still in use in Kenya and Cameroon. These concerning chemicals are readily available to both small- and large-scale farmers, despite them being unaware of their effects.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
TIMOSOARA / SZEGED - Industrial pig farms report clean environmental papers, but nearby residents complain of odours and pollution, while groundwater shows nitrate contamination, and monitoring relies on self-reported data.

Pig farming in Romania and Hungary is becoming increasingly intensive and centralized, with hundreds of thousands of tons of pork produced annually and the largest companies operating under environmental permits that present the sector as strictly regulated and properly monitored. On paper, the farms we investigated almost never exceeded pollution indicators for air, water or soil. In the villages
around them, however, residents repeatedly complained about heavy odours, manure spreading and we found a recurring sense of discontent with the activities of industrial pig farms.

We reviewed hundreds of documents, interviewed experts and authorities, and visited pig farms and the main slaughterhouse in Western Romania. We found that several groundwater bodies beneath or near pig farming areas are affected by nitrate pollution. We also uncovered a monitoring system that relies heavily on self-monitoring: farms collect their own environmental test samples, contract the laboratory for analyses, and authorities mainly check the paperwork. The result is a bureaucratic chain that transforms a contested reality into perfect paperwork.

Key findings:

  • Several groundwater bodies beneath pig farming areas in both Romania and Hungary are polluted, spanning at least two counties in Romania and confirmed by Romanian Waters Authority reports naming specific companies, including a Chinese-owned local firm and Smithfield, as potential polluters of three groundwater bodies.
  • The area of groundwater bodies linked to Smithfield's agricultural and livestock activities covers 14,625 square kilometres — roughly twice the size of Timiș county.
  • Both countries rely on a self-monitoring system: farms collect their own wastewater and manure samples, pay and contract the laboratories that analyse them, and state authorities largely review only the paperwork submitted by the farms themselves, without independent verification.
  • In Hungary, the national authority issued only one fine — 700 euros — in the past five years, for a farm operating outside the terms of its integrated environmental permit.
  • A soil expert (Alina Bădilă, Association of Soil Experts) states that nothing in current certification regulation prevents farms from requesting analyses tailored to produce favourable results, since no independent body verifies sampling integrity.
  • Residents near industrial farms and the Utvin slaughterhouse (Comtim/WH Group, near Timișoara) report persistent odours and a fish die-off in the Bega river, which authorities attributed to natural causes (heat and oxygen depletion) rather than discharges, despite a roughly 30 cm pipe discharging brown water into the river from behind the slaughterhouse.

Methodology:

The investigation combined document review, official data requests, field reporting and expert consultation across Romania and Hungary. The team analysed hundreds of documents, including environmental permits, self-monitoring reports submitted by pig farms, and official reports from Romania's National Administration "Apele Române" (Romanian Waters Authority), which monitors surface and groundwater quality and names specific companies as potential polluters of groundwater bodies. Formal information requests were filed with Romania's National Environmental Guard and National Agency for Environmental Protection and Protected Areas, as well as with Hungarian authorities including the Csongrád-Csanád County Government Office, covering sanctions, fines, permits and environmental incidents over the past decade. Field visits included ten industrial pig farms and the main slaughterhouse in Western Romania (Timiș and Arad counties), as well as an industrial farm near Szeged, Hungary. The team interviewed experts, authorities, industry representatives, local NGOs, and residents, including a soil expert from the Association of Soil Experts (part of the OSPA network of Pedological and Agrochemical Study Offices), who raised concerns about the independence of farm-commissioned soil and water analyses. Cross-border coordination between the Romanian (Context) and Hungarian (Átlátszó) reporters was maintained through weekly meetings throughout the project.

Themes

  • Agriculture
  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • The parallel reality of intensive pig-farming in Hungary and Romania: Heavy pollution of the groundwaters covered by a bureaucratic scheme, Context, 08/07/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Romania
  • Hungary

Matei Capota

Matei Capota is a Romanian journalist at Context.ro.

Oana Maniţiu

Oana Maniţiu is a Romanian journalist at Context.ro.

Attila Biro

Attila Biro is the Romania-based investigative journalist and the co-founder of CONTEXT.

Csaba Segesvári

Csaba Segesvári is a Hungarian journalist.

Media

The Context platform is an independent Romanian media start-up.

Átlátszó Hungary

Atlatszo is a Hungarian investigative journalism non-profit organisation.

Related projects

  • © Selen Magnolia Gatti

    Living Under the Veiled Grasp of Factory Farming in Europe

    PENFOUL - 142 million pigs, 76 million bovine heads, 62 million sheep, and 12 million goats: the invisible yearly population of farmed animals that live and die on the production line in Europe. Industrial livestock farming across Europe is causing widespread environmental degradation. People living in close proximity to factory farms experience serious health consequences.

    Meer lezen
  • © Niall Sargent, Noteworthy

    Hidden cross-border pollution in Ireland and the United Kingdom

    BELFAST - As part of a cross-border project to investigate the poultry industry on the island of Ireland, the investigative team from The Detail, Noteworthy and The Guardian took a deep dive into cross-border litter trade and the environmental impacts from the industry as it expands in line with State policy.

    Meer lezen
  • © Aïda Grovestins

    Feeding Europe's Farms, Emptying Africa's Seas

    KAYAR - Over half a million tonnes of fish are turned into fishmeal and fish oil to feed animals in industrial aquaculture systems and on intensive farms and demand is growing, as is outrage in West African fishing communities.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
ROME / MADRID / LONDON - In Italy, Spain and the UK, meat, eggs and dairy are increasingly produced by large corporations that use industrial farming methods and wield growing power over multibillion-euro supply chains. For animals, more industrial farming usually means more suffering.

For people, economists warn, the risk of corporate consolidation is that cost savings are converted into profits rather than lower prices, even as payments to farmers are squeezed.

Concentration in the meat and dairy sector is a Europe-wide phenomenon that, in the United Kingdom, reaches extremely high levels.

Eight companies control between 70 and 85 per cent of the British meat market (estimated at 22 billion pounds), whilst five companies account for almost 60 per cent of the dairy market (estimated at 11.9 billion). In the pigmeat sector, Cranswick, Karro, Dunbia UK and Pilgrim’s Europe alone control around 90 per cent of the country’s total production, whilst Pilgrim’s Europe also controls around 30 per cent of the chicken meat market.

In Italy, the ten leading companies in the processing of dairy products, meat, sausages and eggs account for 38.1 per cent of the industrial sector of the dairy, poultry, beef and pig supply chains combined. This amounts to €17.2 billion, a considerable figure that illustrates the degree of concentration in this important economic sector, which, according to the Institute for Agricultural and Food Market Services (Ismea), is worth around €45 billion. If we consider meat production alone, the value rises further, with the five largest companies controlling over half (51.7 per cent) of the market, worth just over 12 billion euros.

Many of these Italian companies are part of even larger groups that manage many stages of the meat and dairy supply chains, as part of a process of increasing vertical integration. In most cases, they are owned by Italian families.

In Spain, where the market is growing very rapidly, the situation is similar to that in Italy. In 2024, the total turnover of the meat sector reached 41.34 billion euros, an increase of almost 70 per cent compared with five years earlier. In this context, the top five processing companies accounted for almost 30 per cent of the sector’s total turnover.

The vertical integration of the supply chains is also similar to that in Italy, and even greater. Vall Companys, for example, directly controls feed mills and thousands of livestock farms, slaughtering 5.5 million pigs and 160 million chickens a year. Guissona, which began as a co-operative, has gone on to own a bank and a supermarket chain, BonArea – a move that no major group in Italy has yet made.

Finally, in Spain, as in Italy, the leading meat companies are family-run: eight of the ten largest, in addition to the Italian Pini group. The United Kingdom, on the other hand, stands out in this respect as well: foreign capital controls around 40 per cent of the British meat market and over half of the dairy market.

Image by Laura Villadiego: A large livestock farm in Spain.

  • Agriculture

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
SKOPJE / VRANJE / BONN - This cross border investigation reveals a river system under severe and long term pressure, where local neglect, institutional weakness, and industrial malpractice converge into a single cross border environmental crisis.

Illegal dumpsites choke Macedonia's Vardar river, its rubbish forming dams that divert the flow. Two decades of unchecked dumping have turned a once-batheable river into a health hazard, worsened in late 2025 by floating waste from a mismanaged sports federation. Prosecutions remain rare, and over half of Macedonia's industrial facilities discharge untreated wastewater, largely unmonitored due to reliance on polluters' own labs. A 2016 water law was never implemented, a Skopje corruption case closed without evidence, and EU-funded treatment plants risk missing their deadlines.
Serbia faces the same structural failures despite heavier investment. German-funded plants exist, but land disputes, weak municipal capacity and low tariffs stall progress; the EIB reports similar delays in Skopje and Belgrade. Belgrade alone discharges roughly 190 million cubic metres of wastewater yearly, strained further by hundreds of cruise boats and floating venues, while its own treatment plant keeps losing funding priority to EXPO projects.
Germany's 1986 Rhine disaster offers a counterpoint: it triggered a full overhaul of river governance, proving reform is possible with political will and cross-border cooperation.
The fix is clear: independent monitoring, finished infrastructure, EU-aligned laws and real enforcement. The question is whether the Balkans act before their rivers reach the point of no return.

Photo by Aleksandar Metodijev, Vardar River in Tetovo

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
HOTAZEL - Demand for manganese, a critical mineral for the green transition, has surged in recent years. But in South Africa’s Kalahari basin, home to the world’s largest reserves and a major direct supplier to Europe, mining is depleting and contaminating underground water sources that local communities depend on, causing damage experts warn could last for generations.

Manganese is common in the Earth’s crust and essential in small amounts to human health. But it is also critical to the production of steel, including the steel used in wind turbines, and increasingly important in batteries for electric vehicles, particularly newer-generation technologies. The EU included manganese in its 2024 Critical Raw Materials Act, a list of materials vital to the bloc’s green transition.

South Africa accounts for about a third of global manganese production and holds roughly 70 percent of known reserves. Much of this mineral wealth lies beneath the sands of the Kalahari basin, a vast, arid region straddling South Africa, Namibia and Botswana. More than a quarter of Europe’s direct manganese supply comes from there, and the share is likely higher when indirect imports of processed material are taken into account.

But in the Kalahari, extracting the mineral carries heavy environmental and social costs. What residents describe as a once-pristine landscape of mustard-coloured sand expanses dotted with ancient camel thorn woodlands is now scarred by open-cast craters, tailings dumps and abandoned mine sites. Lines of thundering trucks throw up plumes of toxic dust, and from time-to-time explosive blasts reverberate in the background, followed by puffs of smoke.

Farmers and ranchers say mining is depleting and contaminating underground water sources they depend on. Black communities whose forebears were forcibly resettled almost a century ago say mining companies regularly promise paved roads, youth jobs, street lighting, school facilities and food aid, only to break their word. Residents complain of heavy dust pollution, damaged homes, sick livestock and little lasting benefit from the mineral wealth extracted around them.

“This country is rich because of mines, but we are in a ghetto. All of us stay poor and suffer in a rich land,” one resident said.

Key findings

  • Farmers, residents and hydrological reports point to aquifer depletion linked to mine dewatering, as well as contamination by nitrates and other pollutants. Experts warn that in some areas groundwater systems could take more than a century to recover after mine closure.
  • Villagers around Hotazel report cracked homes from blasting, dust-covered gardens, sick or dying livestock, broken promises from mining companies and limited access to jobs. Several communities trace today’s grievances to older histories of forced resettlement and dispossession.
  • South Africa’s mining laws are formally progressive, but officials, activists and experts describe under-resourced oversight, “window-dressing compliance” and poor attention to cumulative impacts. Smaller mines are seen as especially problematic, while rehabilitation of damaged land remains patchy.

Photo by Madelene Cronjé

Publication

ONLINE

But in South Africa’s Kalahari basin, home to the world’s largest reserves and a major direct supplier to Europe, mining is depleting and contaminating underground water sources that local communities depend on, causing damage experts warn could last for generations.

Manganese is common in the Earth’s crust and essential in small amounts to human health. But it is also critical to the production of steel, including the steel used in wind turbines, and increasingly important in batteries for electric vehicles, particularly newer-generation technologies. The EU included manganese in its 2024 Critical Raw Materials Act, a list of materials vital to the bloc’s green transition.

South Africa accounts for about a third of global manganese production and holds roughly 70 percent of known reserves. Much of this mineral wealth lies beneath the sands of the Kalahari basin, a vast, arid region straddling South Africa, Namibia and Botswana. More than a quarter of Europe’s direct manganese supply comes from there, and the share is likely higher when indirect imports of processed material are taken into account.

But in the Kalahari, extracting the mineral carries heavy environmental and social costs. What residents describe as a once-pristine landscape of mustard-coloured sand expanses dotted with ancient camel thorn woodlands is now scarred by open-cast craters, tailings dumps and abandoned mine sites. Lines of thundering trucks throw up plumes of toxic dust, and from time-to-time explosive blasts reverberate in the background, followed by puffs of smoke.

Farmers and ranchers say mining is depleting and contaminating underground water sources they depend on. Black communities whose forebears were forcibly resettled almost a century ago say mining companies regularly promise paved roads, youth jobs, street lighting, school facilities and food aid, only to break their word. Residents complain of heavy dust pollution, damaged homes, sick livestock and little lasting benefit from the mineral wealth extracted around them.

“This country is rich because of mines, but we are in a ghetto. All of us stay poor and suffer in a rich land,” one resident said.

Key findings

  • Farmers, residents and hydrological reports point to aquifer depletion linked to mine dewatering, as well as contamination by nitrates and other pollutants. Experts warn that in some areas groundwater systems could take more than a century to recover after mine closure.
  • Villagers around Hotazel report cracked homes from blasting, dust-covered gardens, sick or dying livestock, broken promises from mining companies and limited access to jobs. Several communities trace today’s grievances to older histories of forced resettlement and dispossession.
  • South Africa’s mining laws are formally progressive, but officials, activists and experts describe under-resourced oversight, “window-dressing compliance” and poor attention to cumulative impacts. Smaller mines are seen as especially problematic, while rehabilitation of damaged land remains patchy.

Photo by Madelene Cronjé

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
CATALONIA / MAURITIUS – Since China halted exports during the COVID-19 pandemic, Mauritius has become the world's leading exporter of long-tailed macaques for biomedical research, supplying close to half of all animals traded worldwide in 2024.

The Monkey Trade from Mauritius to Europe

Spain is the main EU entry point for the test monkeys. This investigation traces the supply chain from the breeding facilities of the Indian Ocean island to the testing and warehousing sites that hold thousands of the endangered animals on European soil. The reporting exposes the corporate structures behind the trade, the transport routes that move the animals into the EU, and the gap between how the industry justifies itself and what the reporting on the ground reveals.

The reporting centres on Charles River Laboratories, a US biomedical corporation, and on Bioculture, the Mauritius’s largest breeder of long-tailed macaques. The investigation lays bare the economics of the trade: trappers are paid up to €180 per wild-caught animal, while a single macaque now sells to a laboratory for as much as €45,000. And the investigation exposes a truth the industry prefers you not to know: long-tailed macaques, an endangered species, aren’t even required for testing.

Photo by Nathalie Bertrams, Long-tailed macaques from Mauritius in Europe’s largest monkey farm Camarney, Tarragona, Spain

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
ULCINJ / CERVIA – Two salt marshes, two different environmental crises. A cross-border investigation combining satellite imagery, field reporting and environmental economics reveals the hidden costs of wetland degradation across Europe.

Europe has made nature restoration a political priority. But how much does it actually cost to lose an ecosystem? And who ultimately pays the price when restoration comes too late?

Restoration at a Price is a cross-border investigation into two Mediterranean salt marshes that explores a question environmental journalism rarely addresses: can restoring nature be more cost-effective than paying for the consequences of environmental degradation?

Developed by FACTA (Italy) and the Center for Investigative Journalism of Montenegro (CIN-CG), with scientific support from environmental economists Francesco Silvestri and Vincenzo Barone (Eco & Eco), the investigation combines investigative reporting, satellite imagery and environmental economics to examine how biodiversity loss, climate change and governance failures translate into measurable ecological and economic costs.

The investigation focuses on two emblematic case studies.

In Ulcinj (Montenegro), we investigate how a flawed privatisation, years of institutional neglect and unresolved legal disputes transformed the eastern Adriatic's largest salt marsh from a productive landscape into a degraded ecosystem. Through satellite analysis, field reporting and interviews, we document the collapse of the hydraulic system that once sustained one of the Adriatic Flyway's most important stopover sites for migratory birds, while examining how governance failures have delayed restoration despite the site's strategic importance for biodiversity conservation and Montenegro's EU accession process.

In Cervia (Italy), the challenge is different but equally significant. One of the Mediterranean's last active saltworks, Cervia demonstrates how traditional salt production, biodiversity conservation and sustainable tourism can coexist within a protected wetland. The devastating floods of May 2023, however, exposed both the vulnerability of this ecosystem and its crucial role in flood mitigation. The investigation explores whether simply rebuilding damaged infrastructure is the most effective response in an increasingly flood-prone region, or whether restoring wetlands as nature-based solutions could deliver greater long-term environmental and economic benefits.

Together, these stories show that the cost of environmental degradation extends far beyond restoration works. By connecting local investigations with broader European debates on nature restoration, climate adaptation and ecosystem services, the project asks whether investing in healthy wetlands should be considered not simply an environmental obligation, but a long-term public investment.

Key findings
Mediterranean salt marshes are socio-ecological systems whose ecological functioning depends on active water management.

  • In Ulcinj (Montenegro), a flawed privatisation followed by more than a decade of institutional neglect has resulted in ecological degradation alongside economic losses exceeding €40 million. Since salt production stopped in 2013, Montenegro has lost an estimated 187,000 tonnes of salt (worth around €19 million), while restoring the hydraulic system is expected to require a further €19 million. Satellite imagery and ecological monitoring document declining salinity, habitat degradation and the collapse of one of the Adriatic Flyway's key migratory bird stopover sites.
  • In Cervia (Italy), the 2023 floods demonstrated both the vulnerability of coastal salt marshes to climate change and their strategic role in flood mitigation. The investigation questions whether rebuilding damaged infrastructure as it was before is economically sustainable in one of Italy's most flood-prone regions, arguing that wetland restoration should instead be integrated into climate adaptation strategies as a nature-based solution.
    Environmental economics makes it possible to estimate not only restoration costs, but also the hidden value of ecosystem services that are rarely considered in public decision-making.
    Delaying restoration increases both ecological damage and long-term economic costs, making early investment in healthy wetlands more effective than paying for the consequences of environmental decline.

Methodology

Following FACTA's method, that applies the scientific methodology to investigative and data journalism, the project combines investigative journalism with scientific research and environmental-economic assessment. The reporting integrates a systematic review of scientific literature and policy documents, high-resolution satellite imagery from Planet Labs and the Copernicus Sentinel constellation, field reporting in Italy and Montenegro, and interviews with researchers, former saltworks workers, environmental organisations, public authorities and local communities.

To complement the journalistic investigation, eco&eco developed an environmental-economic framework to assess the hidden costs of salt marsh degradation and restoration. Rather than assigning a market price to nature, the analysis estimates the value of ecosystem services - including biodiversity conservation, flood regulation, carbon storage and climate resilience - and compares these benefits with the costs of environmental degradation and delayed restoration. The project combines Earth observation, investigative reporting and environmental economics to develop a replicable methodology for investigating wetland restoration across Europe.

Images:

1. The abandoned warehouse in the degraded Ulcinj Saltworks. © CIN-CG

2. The Cervia Saltworks flooded after the 2023 Emilia-Romagna floods. © Planet Labs / FACTA.EU
